chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 2(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the statutory term "assessment" includes which of the following?
options: Only the physical examination and classification of goods
Only re-assessment ordered by appellate authorities
Provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment and any assessment where duty is assessed as nil
Only the determination of duty payable on imported goods
explain: Section 2(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 defines "assessment" broadly to include provisional assessment, self-assessment, re-assessment, and any order of assessment in which the duty assessed is nil. (Source: Bare Act & R.K. Jain Customs Law Manual)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 2(2)

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 2(24) of the Customs Act, 1962 , "imported goods" cease to be imported goods when:
options: They cross the territorial waters of India
They are unloaded at the customs port or airport
They are cleared for home consumption
They are deposited into a public bonded warehouse
explain: Under Section 2(24), "imported goods" means any goods brought into India from a place outside India but does not include goods which have been cleared for home consumption. Once out of charge for home consumption is granted, they lose their imported character. (Source: CBIC / Section 2(24))
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 2(24)

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: How does Section 2(33) of the Customs Act, 1962 define "prohibited goods"?
options: Goods imported without an Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)
Any goods the import or export of which is subject to any prohibition under this Act or any other law, but does not include goods where conditions have been satisfied
Only narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances
Any goods completely banned from trade under Indian penal statutes only
explain: Section 2(33) defines prohibited goods as goods whose import or export is prohibited under the Customs Act or any other law for the time being in force, but expressly excludes goods in respect of which the conditions of import/export have been complied with. (Source: Section 2(33) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 2(33)

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 7 of the Customs Act, 1962 , the statutory authority empowered to appoint customs ports, customs airports, and Inland Container Depots (ICDs) is:
options: The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways directly
The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), by notification in the Official Gazette
The Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)
The State Government having maritime jurisdiction
explain: Under Section 7(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the Board (CBIC) is empowered, by notification in the Official Gazette, to appoint customs ports, airports, inland container depots (ICDs), and land customs stations. (Source: CBIC / Section 7)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 7

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Which section of the Customs Act, 1962 operates as the primary charging section for the levy of customs duties on goods?
explain: Section ₹2 is the charging section of the Customs Act, 1962 . It provides that duties of customs shall be levied at specified rates on goods imported into, or exported from, India, as provided under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 or other applicable laws. (Source: R.K. Jain Customs Law Manual)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 12

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section ₹3 of the Customs Act, 1962 , if imported goods are pilfered after unloading thereof and before an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse:
options: The importer must pay duty but can claim full refund within 30 days
The shipping line must pay double the duty assessed
The importer is not liable to pay duty, and under Section 45(3) the custodian is liable to pay duty
Duty is abated in proportion to the value of remaining cargo
explain: Under Section ₹3 , the importer is completely exonerated from paying duty on pilfered goods. Furthermore, under Section 45(3), the custodian of the goods is statutorily liable to pay duty on such pilfered goods. Section ₹3 does not apply if goods are restored or if pilferage occurs after clearance. (Source: Section ₹3 & Section 45(3) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 13

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section ₹5 (1)(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the rate of duty and tariff valuation applicable to imported goods cleared for home consumption under Section 46 shall be the rate in force on:
options: The date of sailing from the load port abroad
The date on which the goods are physically examined at the dock
The date of payment of duty in the bank
The date of presentation of the Bill of Entry or the date of entry inwards of the vessel, whichever is later
explain: Section ₹5 (1)(a) mandates that for goods entered for home consumption, the relevant rate of duty and tariff valuation is that in force on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry, or the date of arrival/entry inwards of the conveyance, whichever is later. (Source: CBIC / Section ₹5 (1)(a))
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 15(1)(a)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section ₹5 (1)(b) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the relevant date for determining the rate of duty on goods cleared from a bonded warehouse for home consumption is:
options: The date of deposit of goods into the warehouse
The date when the warehousing period of 1 year expires
The date of filing of the Into-Bond Bill of Entry (Space / Yellow Bill)
The date on which the Ex-Bond Bill of Entry for home consumption is presented under Section 68
explain: Section ₹5 (1)(b) provides that in the case of warehoused goods cleared for home consumption under Section 68, the rate of duty and tariff valuation is that in force on the date on which a Bill of Entry for home consumption in respect of such goods is presented. (Source: Section ₹5 (1)(b) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 15(1)(b)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section ₹6 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the rate of duty and tariff valuation applicable to export goods entered under a Shipping Bill shall be the rate in force on:
options: The date on which foreign exchange proceeds are realized
The date of issuance of the Mate Receipt by the ship master
The date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading (Let Export Order) under Section 51
The date of filing the Shipping Bill electronically on ICEGATE
explain: Under Section ₹6 (1)(a), the rate of duty for export goods is the rate in force on the date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods (Let Export Order) under Section 51. (Source: Section ₹6 (1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 16(1)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section ₹7 of the Customs Act, 1962 , how is the primary assessment of duty conducted on imported or export goods?
options: Provisional assessment with mandatory bank guarantee
Self-assessment by the importer or exporter, subject to verification by the Proper Officer via Risk Management System (RMS)
Assessment conducted exclusively by the Custodian
Compulsory assessment by the Assistant Commissioner in every case
explain: Section ₹7 (1) establishes the regime of self-assessment whereby the importer or exporter self-assesses duty. Under Section ₹7 (2), the proper officer may verify the self-assessment, selecting entries based on risk evaluation criteria (RMS). (Source: Section ₹7 Customs Act, 1962 / CBIC Circulars)
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 17

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Which of the following is a valid statutory ground for ordering a Provisional Assessment under Section ₹8 of the Customs Act, 1962 ?
options: Chemical or other tests are required, or further inquiry/documents are necessary, or valuation cannot be immediately determined
The importer requests extra time to pay assessed duty without interest
The Customs Broker forgot to sign the digital declaration
The goods are banned under the Foreign Trade Policy
explain: Section ₹8 (1) permits provisional assessment where chemical/other tests are pending, where the importer/exporter has not produced necessary documents, or where the proper officer deems it necessary to make further inquiry to determine duty or valuation, subject to execution of a bond. (Source: Section ₹8 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 18

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 23(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , remission of duty on imported goods is permissible where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner that goods have been:
options: Exported without payment of IGST under LUT
Cleared without physical examination by mistake
Pilfered while stored in a private bonded warehouse
Lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption
explain: Section 23(1) governs remission where goods are lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed (such as by accidental fire, flood, or natural disaster) at any time before clearance for home consumption. (Source: Section 23(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(1)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , an owner may relinquish title to imported goods and avoid payment of duty thereon, provided:
options: Relinquishment is made before an order for clearance for home consumption (Sec 47) or deposit in warehouse (Sec 60), and no offence appears to have been committed
The goods have already been taken out of customs custody
The importer pays a mandatory penalty of 25% of the cargo value
Relinquishment is done within 1 year from the date of import manifest
explain: Section 23(2) allows the owner of imported goods to relinquish title before an order for clearance for home consumption under Section 47 or deposit in warehouse under Section 60, whereupon duty liability ceases, provided no offence has been committed in respect of such goods. (Source: Section 23(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(2)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 22 of the Customs Act, 1962 , how is duty abated on imported goods that have been damaged or deteriorated before or during unloading?
options: Abatement is granted only if damage exceeds 75% of invoice value
Duty is abated in proportion to the diminution in the value of the goods (Duty = Full Duty x Value after damage / Value before damage)
Duty is completely waived and goods are returned to exporter
Duty is reduced to a flat 5% ad valorem
explain: Under Section 22(1) & 22(2), duty on damaged/deteriorated goods is charged in proportion to the reduced value: Duty Payable = Full Duty on sound goods x (Value of damaged goods / Value of sound goods). (Source: Section 22 Customs Act, 1962 / R.K. Jain)
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 22

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the standard limitation period for filing an application for refund of customs duty paid by an individual or importer?
options: 3 years from the end of the financial year
1 year from the date of payment of duty or interest
6 months from the date of clearance
30 days from the date of final assessment
explain: Under Section 27(1), any person claiming refund of duty or interest paid must make an application before the expiry of 1 year from the date of payment of such duty or interest, subject to the doctrine of unjust enrichment under Section 27(2). (Source: Section 27 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 27

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what are the respective statutory time limits for issuing a Show Cause Notice (SCN) for recovery of duty in normal cases versus cases involving collusion, wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
explain: Under Section 28, the proper officer can serve an SCN within 2 years from the relevant date in normal cases (amended by Finance Act 2016), and within 5 years where duty was not levied/short-levied by reason of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. (Source: Section 28 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 28AA of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the notified annual rate of interest payable on delayed payment of customs duty?
explain: Notification No. 33/2016-Customs (N.T.) notified the rate of interest under Section 28AA at ₹5 % per annum for delayed payment of customs duty. (Source: CBIC / Section 28AA)
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28AA

chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
text: Under Section 30 of the Customs Act, 1962 , an Arrival Manifest or Import Manifest (IGM) in respect of a vessel or aircraft carrying imported goods must be delivered electronically:
options: At the discretion of the master before port clearance
Prior to the arrival of the vessel or aircraft at the customs port or airport
Within 24 hours after anchoring at the berth
Within 7 days of completion of discharge
explain: Section 30(1) requires the person-in-charge of a vessel or aircraft to deliver an electronic arrival manifest/import report prior to the arrival of the conveyance, in the prescribed form. (Source: Section 30 Customs Act, 1962 / Sea Cargo Manifest Regs)
topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Section 30

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 , an importer is required to present a Bill of Entry before the end of the next day following the day of arrival of the conveyance. If filed late without approved cause, what late fee is leviable?
options: ₹2,500 per day up to a maximum of ₹25,000
Flat 1% of the assessable value per day
₹5,000 per day for the initial three days, and Rs ₹0,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay
explain: Under the second proviso to Section 46(3) read with Bill of Entry Regulations, late presentation charges are ₹5,000 per day for the first three days, and Rs ₹0,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay. (Source: CBIC Circular No. ₹2 /2017-Cus & Section 46(3))
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3)

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 47(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , once an electronic Bill of Entry is returned to the importer for payment of duty, the importer must pay the assessed duty within:
options: 48 hours from arrival of the vessel
The same day or by the next day (excluding holidays) of return of the Bill of Entry, failing which interest at ₹5 % is payable
explain: Section 47(2) mandates that the importer shall pay the duty within the same day or by the next day (excluding holidays) of the date on which the Bill of Entry is returned to him for payment. Delay attracts interest under Section 28AA. (Source: Section 47(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 47(2)

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962 , if imported goods are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused within what time period from unloading may the custodian, after notice, sell them with customs permission?
explain: Section 48 provides that if any goods brought into India are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within 30 days from the date of unloading (or extended period), the person having custody may, after notice to the importer and with permission of customs, sell them. (Source: Section 48 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 48

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 58A of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is a "Special Warehouse"?
options: A warehouse for storing notified goods (e.g. duty-free shops, ship stores, crude petroleum) under the physical lock and key of customs
A private warehouse for non-dutiable cargo
A transit shed operated by the Port Authority
explain: Section 58A empowers the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner to license a special warehouse wherein physical lock and custody of customs is maintained. Goods notified under Sec 58A include duty-free shop goods, supply to foreign-going vessels/aircrafts, and specified sensitive goods. (Source: Section 58A Customs Act, 1962 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 58A

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 59(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the monetary liability of the warehousing bond executed by an importer before warehousing goods?
options: Equal to the assessable CIF value of the goods
Equal to the duty plus ₹8 % interest
Twice the basic customs duty only
A sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed on such goods
explain: Section 59(1) mandates the execution of a bond binding the importer in a sum equal to thrice the amount of duty assessed on the goods, undertaking to observe all warehousing rules and pay duty, interest, and penalties. (Source: Section 59(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 59

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 61 of the Customs Act, 1962 , for how long may goods (other than capital goods for EOUs / MOOWR) remain warehoused without interest on duty becoming payable?
options: 90 days from the date of deposit in warehouse
explain: Section 61(2) specifies that where warehoused goods remain in a warehouse beyond a period of 90 days from the date of deposit, interest at the notified rate (₹5 % p.a.) is payable on the duty from the expiry of the said 90 days till clearance. (Source: Section 61(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 61

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: The MOOWR Scheme (Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations) is framed under which section of the Customs Act, 1962 ?
explain: Section 65 allows manufacture and other operations in a bonded warehouse with permission. Under the revamped MOOWR regulations, imported capital goods and raw materials enjoy duty deferment until cleared into DTA or duty exemption if exported. (Source: Section 65 Customs Act, 1962 / MOOWR Regs 2019)
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 65

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹08 of the Customs Act, 1962 , statements recorded during summons before a Gazetted Officer of Customs:
options: Can only be taken in the presence of the examinee's advocate as a matter of absolute right
Are deemed to be recorded in a judicial proceeding within the meaning of Sections ₹93 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code
Expire after 30 days if an FIR is not registered
Are inadmissible hearsay evidence in any court of law
explain: Section ₹08 (4) provides that all persons summoned are bound to state the truth, and an inquiry under Section ₹08 is deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of Section ₹93 and Section 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). (Source: Section ₹08 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962 prescribes a mandatory equal penalty (₹00 % of duty and interest) in which category of contraventions?
options: Every procedural delay in filing Bill of Entry
Technical errors in digital signature certificates on ICEGATE
Short-levy or non-levy of duty or erroneous refund by reason of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts
Baggage declarations with valuation errors below ₹5,000
explain: Section 114A imposes a mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest not levied, short-levied or erroneously refunded where such non-levy is by reason of collusion or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. If paid within 30 days with duty and interest, penalty is reduced to 25%. (Source: Section 114A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114A

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: What is the maximum penalty leviable under Section 114AA of the Customs Act, 1962 for knowingly using false and incorrect material or declarations?
options: Up to five times the value of the goods
Up to double the assessable value
explain: Section 114AA penalizes intentional use of false or incorrect declarations, statements or documents with a penalty up to five times the value of the goods (specifically enacted to combat invoice fraud and fraudulent export claims). (Source: Section 114AA Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114AA

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹25 of the Customs Act, 1962 , when goods are confiscated, the adjudicating officer may give an option to pay a redemption fine in lieu of confiscation. What is the statutory ceiling on such fine?
options: It cannot exceed 25% of the CIF value
It shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon
There is no ceiling; it is at absolute discretion of the officer
It cannot exceed the Basic Customs Duty
explain: The proviso to Section ₹25 (1) stipulates that the fine in lieu of confiscation shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon. (Source: Section ₹25 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 125

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: What is the statutory time limit for filing an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) under Section ₹28 , and what is the mandatory pre-deposit required under Section 129E?
options: 60 days (extendable by 30 days on sufficient cause); mandatory pre-deposit of 7.5% of duty demanded or penalty
explain: Section ₹28 (1) allows 60 days to appeal to Commissioner (Appeals), with 30 days condonation power. Section 129E mandates a pre-deposit of 7.5% of duty demanded or penalty imposed for maintaining the appeal before Commissioner (Appeals). (Source: Section ₹28 & 129E Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 128 & Section 129E

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 129A of the Customs Act, 1962 , which of the following matters decided by a Commissioner (Appeals) is specifically EXCLUDED from the appellate jurisdiction of CESTAT (and goes to Central Government revision under Sec 129DD)?
options: Valuation of chemical inputs under CVR 2007
Baggage, drawback, and shortage of goods in conveyances
explain: The first proviso to Section 129A(1) excludes orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) relating to (a) loss of goods/shortage in conveyance, (b) baggage, and (c) drawback under Chapter X. These are reviewable by the Central Government under Section 129DD Revision. (Source: Section 129A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹35 of the Customs Act, 1962 , in cases of duty evasion or fraudulent evasion of prohibitions where the value/duty involved exceeds ₹50 Lakhs, the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to:
explain: Section ₹35 (1)(i) provides that in cases of goods involving duty evasion exceeding ₹50 Lakhs, or prohibited goods under Section ₹1 , the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 7 years and with fine. (Source: Section ₹35 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 135

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , on what base value is Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) calculated on imported goods?
options: Assessable Value (CIF) plus Basic Customs Duty (BCD) plus any other applicable customs duties/cesses (except IGST and GST Cess)
explain: Under Section 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , the value for levying IGST under Section 3(7) is the assessable value determined under Section ₹4 plus Basic Customs Duty and all other duties of customs leviable, excluding IGST and GST Compensation Cess. (Source: Section 3(7)/(8) CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 3(7)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Section 9A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , what is Anti-Dumping Duty and what is its statutory validity duration unless revoked earlier?
options: A duty equal to the margin of dumping (Normal Value minus Export Price) to offset market injury, remaining in force for 5 years from notification
A permanent non-expiring duty on all Chinese products
A penalty levied by the Port Trust on unexamined containers
A duty on export of raw materials valid for 1 year
explain: Under Section 9A(1) & 9A(5), Anti-Dumping Duty is levied to counteract dumping (margin = Normal Value in exporting country minus Export Price). It ceases to have effect on the expiry of 5 years from the date of imposition, unless extended via sunset review. (Source: Section 9A CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 9A

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: According to General Interpretative Rule (GIR) 1 of the Import Tariff, titles of Sections, Chapters, and Sub-Chapters:
options: Have overriding statutory force over Chapter Notes
Can be ignored if the Customs Broker prefers another classification
Are provided for ease of reference only, and legal classification is determined strictly according to the terms of the headings and relative Section/Chapter Notes
Are binding only in anti-dumping investigations
explain: GIR 1 establishes that titles are for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes. (Source: GIR Rule 1 / R.K. Jain Customs Tariff)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 1

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under GIR Rule 2(a), how are incomplete, unfinished, or unassembled/disassembled articles (such as CKD/SKD kits) classified?
options: They must be classified piece by piece under separate tariff lines
Under the heading of raw steel or plastic according to weight
Under the heading of the complete or finished article, provided as presented they have the essential character of the complete or finished article
explain: GIR 2(a) provides that any reference to an article shall be taken to include an incomplete or unfinished article, provided it has the essential character of the complete article; it also applies to complete articles presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD). (Source: GIR Rule 2(a))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 2(a)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under GIR Rule 3(a), when goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, which rule of precedence applies?
options: The heading with the highest basic customs duty rate
Alphabetical order of the tariff description
The heading that appears first in numerical order
The heading providing a more specific description is preferred over headings providing a more general description
explain: GIR 3(a) states that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description (e.g. electric shavers under 85.₹0 rather than electro-mechanical domestic appliances under 85.09). (Source: GIR Rule 3(a))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 3(a)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: When goods cannot be classified by reference to GIR Rule 3(a) (specific description) or GIR Rule 3(b) (essential character), how are they classified under GIR Rule 3(c)?
options: Under the heading with the lowest combined tax rate
Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
Under the heading chosen by the importer
explain: GIR 3(c) mandates that when goods cannot be classified by 3(a) or 3(b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration. (Source: GIR Rule 3(c))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 3(c)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under GIR Rule 5(a), camera cases, musical instrument cases, and specially fitted containers presented with the articles they are intended for:
options: Are always completely exempt from customs duty
Are classified with such articles if specially shaped/fitted, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles, unless the container gives the whole its essential character
Are classified under the container's own raw material heading
Must be classified separately under in all circumstances
explain: GIR 5(a) provides that specially shaped/fitted containers suitable for long-term use (e.g. violin case, camera case) presented with the articles are classified with those articles, unless the container imparts the essential character to the whole. (Source: GIR Rule 5(a))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR Rule 5(a)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹0 (1)(a)(i) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, which category of commission is specifically EXCLUDED from being added to the transaction value?
options: Selling commissions paid to foreign brokers
Royalties and license fees paid as a condition of sale
Buying commissions paid by the buyer to his purchasing agent abroad
Brokerage paid to a freight forwarder
explain: Rule ₹0 (1)(a)(i) explicitly mandates the addition of commissions and brokerage, "except buying commissions". A buying commission paid by an importer to his agent for representation abroad does not form part of the assessable value. (Source: Rule ₹0 (1) CVR 2007 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 & Rule 10(1)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹0 (2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, where the actual cost of transport and insurance from the port of shipment to India are not ascertainable, what statutory percentages of FOB value apply?
options: Transport: 20% of FOB; Insurance: 1.₹25 % of FOB
Transport: 25% of FOB; Insurance: 0.5% of FOB
Transport: ₹5 % of FOB; Insurance: 1% of FOB
explain: Under Rule ₹0 (2), if sea/air freight is not ascertainable, it is taken as 20% of FOB. If insurance is not ascertainable, it is computed at 1.₹25 % of FOB. (Note: 1% landing charges were omitted in 2017). (Source: Rule ₹0 (2) CVR 2007 / Notification 91/2017-Cus (N.T.))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what is the sequence between Rule 7 (Deductive Value) and Rule 8 (Computed Value)?
options: Neither rule can be applied unless CESTAT gives prior sanction
Rule 7 applies only to related party transactions
The order of application of Rule 7 and Rule 8 can be reversed at the request of the importer and with the approval of the Proper Officer
explain: The proviso to Rule 3(4) of CVR 2007 explicitly states that at the request of the importer and with the approval of the proper officer, the order of application of rules 7 and 8 may be reversed. (Source: CVR 2007 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 7 & Rule 8

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹2 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, when the Proper Officer has reasonable doubt as to the truth or accuracy of the declared value, he must:
options: Directly double the assessable value under the residual method
Call for further information/evidence, and if doubt persists, inform the grounds to the importer in writing and provide an opportunity of being heard before rejecting transaction value
Refer the matter to the Directorate General of Valuation within 24 hours
Immediately seize the goods without hearing
explain: Rule ₹2 prescribes the procedure for rejection of declared value: the officer asks for documents/explanation, and if reasonable doubt persists, gives grounds in writing and provides a reasonable opportunity of being heard before proceeding to sequential valuation methods. (Source: Rule ₹2 CVR 2007 / R.K. Jain)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 12

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Section ₹1 (2) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, ₹992 , what is the maximum statutory penalty for contravening the provisions of the Act, Rules, or Foreign Trade Policy?
options: Suspension of driving license of the exporter
Not less than Rs ₹0,000 and not exceeding five times the value of the goods or services or technology in respect of which contravention is made
explain: Section ₹1 (2) of the FTDR Act, ₹992 prescribes that the penalty shall not be less than Rs ₹0,000 and not exceed five times the value of the goods, services, or technology in respect of which the contravention has been made or attempted. (Source: Section ₹1 FTDR Act, ₹992 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 7 & Section 11

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: What is the unique policy duration feature introduced in the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023 compared to earlier Foreign Trade Policies?
options: It applies only to export of agricultural items
It is dynamic and open-ended with no end date, subject to continuous updates as per global trade dynamics
It has a strict 3-year sunset clause
It requires annual parliamentary re-enactment every April
explain: FTP 2023 departed from the traditional 5-year fixed cycle; it is an open-ended, dynamic policy document designed to be updated continuously based on feedback and global economic trends. (Source: DGFT / FTP 2023 Preamble)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Chapter 1 — Legal Framework

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under of FTP 2023, what is the minimum value addition generally prescribed for exports under the Advance Authorisation Scheme, and what are the standard validity periods for import and export obligation?
options: Value Addition: 50%; Import: ₹8 months; Export Obligation: 24 months
Value Addition: 33%; Import: 6 months; Export Obligation: ₹2 months
Value Addition: 5%; Import: 24 months; Export Obligation: 36 months
Value Addition: ₹5 % (except tea 50%); Import Validity: ₹2 months; Export Obligation Period: ₹8 months
explain: Under Paragraph 4.09 of FTP 2023, the minimum value addition is ₹5 % (except for tea where it is 50%). Validity for import is ₹2 months from the date of issue, and the standard Export Obligation Period (EOP) is ₹8 months. (Source: FTP 2023 & HBP Para 4.09/4.40)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Advance Authorisation Scheme

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under of FTP 2023, what is the minimum value addition required for Duty Free Import Authorisation (DFIA), and can the DFIA be transferred to other parties?
options: Minimum 20% value addition; transferable after the export obligation has been discharged and endorsement made by DGFT
Minimum 50% value addition; transferable only to SEZ units
Minimum ₹5 % value addition; transferable immediately on issuance
explain: Paragraph 4.25 of FTP 2023 requires a minimum value addition of 20% for DFIA. Once export obligation is fulfilled and export proceeds are realized, the DFIA and/or imported materials are freely transferable. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 4.25 / 4.27)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — DFIA Scheme

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under the Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme in FTP 2023, what is the export obligation requirement for capital goods imported at zero customs duty?
options: Export obligation equal to 8 times the FOB value in 8 years
Export obligation equivalent to 6 times of duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled in 6 years from authorization date, while maintaining average export turnover
Equal to the CIF value of capital goods within 3 years
Equal to 2 times the duty saved, with no turnover condition
explain: Paragraph 5.01 of FTP 2023 provides that capital goods can be imported at zero customs duty under EPCG, subject to an export obligation equivalent to 6 times the duties, taxes and cesses saved, to be fulfilled within 6 years, over and above maintaining the average export performance. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 5.01)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Chapter 5 — EPCG Scheme

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: What special concession in Export Obligation is granted under the EPCG Scheme of FTP 2023 for units manufacturing green technology products (e.g. solar cells, EV vehicles, rainwater harvesting)?
options: Capital goods can be sold in DTA without any export obligation
Full cash subsidy of 50% of machine value
Export obligation period is extended to ₹5 years
explain: Under Paragraph 5.₹1 of FTP 2023, for exporters manufacturing green technology products (like solar power, wind turbines, electric vehicles), the export obligation is reduced by 25% (i.e. EO is 75% of normal EO). (Source: FTP 2023 Para 5.₹1 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Green Technology Concession

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: What are the revised export performance thresholds (in FOB US$ million over the current plus 3 preceding financial years) for 1-Star to 5-Star Export Houses under FTP 2023?
explain: FTP 2023 rationalized the Status Holder export thresholds: One Star ($3 Million), Two Star ($₹5 Million), Three Star ($50 Million), Four Star ($200 Million), and Five Star ($800 Million). Double weightage is given to MSMEs and women entrepreneurs. (Source: FTP 2023 Table 1.3)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Chapter 1 — Status Recognition

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Which of the following is an authorized operational privilege granted to Status Holders under FTP 2023?
options: Exemption from filing Bill of Entry on imports
Exemption from payment of GST on domestic sales
Right to retain ₹00 % foreign exchange in cash at home
Authorization to self-certify Certificate of Origin (non-preferential) and exemption from furnishing Bank Guarantee under FTP duty exemption schemes
explain: Paragraph 1.26 of FTP 2023 grants Status Holders the privilege of self-certification of origin, ₹00 % exemption from furnishing Bank Guarantees under duty exemption schemes, priority customs clearance, and preferential treatment. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 1.26)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Privileges of Status Holders

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: What is the purpose of the RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products) Scheme under of FTP 2023?
options: To provide a direct export subsidy illegal under WTO rules
To remit embedded central, state, and local duties/taxes (such as electricity duty, VAT on fuel, stamp duty) not refunded under any other mechanism, via electronic transferable scrips on ICEGATE
To provide zero-interest export credit loans
To refund Basic Customs Duty paid on capital goods
explain: Paragraph 4.54 of FTP 2023 outlines RoDTEP as a WTO-compliant mechanism to rebate unrefunded central, state, and local levies embedded in exported products, issued as electronic transferable duty credit scrips in the ICEGATE ledger. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 4.54)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — RoDTEP Scheme

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: What does "SCOMET" stand for under the Foreign Trade Policy and Indian trade regulations?
options: Standard Commodity Organization for Maritime and Electronic Trade
Standard Customs Operations for Marine Export Transport
Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies (dual-use items regulated for international security)
Strategic Committee on Monetary and Exchange Transactions
explain: SCOMET stands for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies. Found in Appendix 3 of Schedule 2 of ITC(HS), these items are dual-use goods whose export is strictly controlled or prohibited. (Source: Chapter ₹0 FTP 2023 / DGFT)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — SCOMET Regulations

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration and Paperless Processing) Regulations, 2018, which form and color designation correspond to a Bill of Entry for Home Consumption?
options: Form II — Yellow Bill of Entry
Form I — White Bill of Entry
Form III — Green Bill of Entry
Form IV — Blue Bill of Entry
explain: Under the regulations and customs procedure: Form I is for Home Consumption (White), Form II is for Warehousing/Into-Bond (Yellow), and Form III is for Ex-Bond clearance for home consumption (Green). (Source: Bill of Entry Regulations 2018 / R.K. Jain)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Forms of Bill of Entry

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 , an Advance or Prior Bill of Entry may be filed up to how many days prior to the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft?
explain: Section 46(3) permits presentation of a Bill of Entry at any time not exceeding 30 days prior to the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft by which the goods have been shipped for importation into India. (Source: Section 46(3) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Advance / Prior Filing

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: In customs manual/EDI documentation practices, what color corresponds to a Duty Drawback Shipping Bill?
explain: Customs EDI / shipping documentation standards designate: White for Free Shipping Bill, Green for Duty Drawback Shipping Bill, Yellow for Dutiable Shipping Bill, and Blue for Export Promotion Schemes (Advance Authorisation / EPCG / EOU). (Source: CBIC Customs Manual)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Color Categorisation of Shipping Bills

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: What is the operational consequence when an electronic Bill of Entry is facilitated under the Risk Management System (RMS) Green Channel?
options: The goods must be examined ₹00 % by the Docks Appraiser
The Bill of Entry is cleared without physical examination and without concurrent assessment by the Appraising Group, moving directly to duty payment and Out of Charge
The importer is exempt from paying IGST
The Bill of Entry must be reviewed by the Commissioner in person
explain: RMS facilitation (Green Channel) allows low-risk consignments to be processed without physical examination or assessment by the Appraising Group, enabling direct duty payment and delivery (Direct Port Delivery / DPD). (Source: CBIC RMS Guidelines / Circular 43/2005)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Green Channel Clearance

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: What is the fundamental procedural difference between "First Check" and "Second Check" examination of imported goods?
options: First check is done by the Customs Broker; second check is done by the importer
First check entails examination and sampling of goods before assessment of duty; second check entails assessment of duty first, followed by examination at the docks before Out of Charge
First check applies only to air cargo; second check applies to sea cargo
First check is optional; second check is governed by the police
explain: Under First Check (requested by importer when parameters/description are unknown), examination occurs before assessment. Under Second Check (the standard default procedure), assessment occurs first, and examination is carried out in the shed/docks before granting Out of Charge. (Source: CBIC Customs Manual / R.K. Jain)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — First Check vs Second Check

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under the CBIC "Turant Customs" initiative, how does Faceless Assessment operate?
options: All imported goods are examined exclusively at the importer's residence
Bills of Entry are assigned anonymously by an automated algorithm to virtual Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs) across the country, delinked from the physical port of import
Assessments are outsourced to private third-party auditing firms
Customs officers inspect cargo wearing biometric visors
explain: Turant Customs introduced Faceless Assessment, whereby Bills of Entry are electronically and randomly routed to virtual Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs) stationed anywhere in India, eliminating physical interface between trade and assessing officers. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 27/2020-Customs)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Faceless Assessment Groups (FAGs)

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: What is "e-Sanchit" on ICEGATE, and what identifier is generated upon uploading supporting documents?
options: An automated payment gateway for paying shipping line detention charges
A portal for tracking vessel speed
A portal for booking truck appointments at ICDs
An online paperless repository for uploading digitally signed PDF supporting documents, which generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN) linked to the declaration
explain: e-Sanchit (electronic Storage and Access of Digitally Signed Supporting Documents) allows paperless filing on ICEGATE. Each uploaded supporting document (invoice, packing list, certificate) generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN). (Source: CBIC Circular No. 40/2017-Customs)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Image Reference Number (IRN)

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under Section 51A of the Customs Act, 1962 , how do importers and Customs Brokers make electronic payments of duty, interest, and penalties on ICEGATE?
options: By sending an account-payee demand draft to CBIC headquarters
By depositing physical cash at the customs cash counter only
By offsetting export incentives directly without ledger entry
Through the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) maintained on the customs automated system
explain: Section 51A mandates the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) on ICEGATE, wherein funds are deposited via net banking/NEFT/RTGS and then utilized to debit and pay customs duties, interest, and penalties electronically. (Source: Section 51A Customs Act, 1962 / Customs ECL Regs 2022)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 74 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what percentage of import duty is granted as drawback when imported duty-paid goods are re-exported as such without being put to any use in India?
explain: Section 74(1) provides that where imported goods are re-exported without being used, 98% of the import duty paid at the time of importation shall be repaid as drawback. (Source: Section 74(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Re-Export of Unused Goods

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Notification No. ₹9 /65-Customs as amended, when imported goods are used before re-export under Section 74, what is the maximum period of use beyond which NO drawback is permissible?
explain: Under Notification No. ₹9 /65-Cus as amended, drawback on goods used before re-export is reduced on a sliding scale for each quarter of use, and where the period of use exceeds ₹8 months, the allowable drawback is NIL. (Source: Notification No. ₹9 /65-Customs as amended)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Notification No. 19/65-Customs (Used Goods)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 74 of the Customs Act, 1962 , imported goods must be entered for export within what time period from the date of payment of duty on importation?
options: 5 years, with permission of the Port Trust
2 years, extendable by the Board (CBIC) on sufficient cause shown
explain: Section 74(1) mandates that the goods must be entered for export within 2 years from the date of payment of duty on the importation thereof, subject to extension by CBIC on sufficient cause shown. (Source: Section 74(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Statutory Time Limit for Section 74

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
section: All Industry Rates vs Brand Rate
text: Under Rule 6 and Rule 7 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, when may an exporter apply for fixation of a Brand Rate or Special Brand Rate of duty drawback?
options: Only for goods exported to SAARC countries
Only when export goods are manufactured in an SEZ
Where the export product has no All Industry Rate (AIR), or where the AIR covers less than four-fifths (80%) of the actual duties paid on inputs
Whenever the exporter prefers cash payment over scrips
explain: Under Rules 6 and 7 of the Drawback Rules 2017, Brand Rate is fixed when an item does not figure in the AIR schedule, or where the exporter demonstrates that the notified AIR drawback covers less than 80% (four-fifths) of the duties actually paid on imported/domestic inputs. (Source: Drawback Rules 2017 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — All Industry Rates vs Brand Rate

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 76 of the Customs Act, 1962 , duty drawback shall NOT be allowed in which of the following circumstances?
options: If the export invoice is denominated in Euros
If goods are exported by air
If the market price of the export goods is less than the amount of drawback claimed, or if the claim is less than ₹50
If the exporter is a merchant exporter rather than a manufacturer
explain: Section 76(1) bars drawback in respect of any goods the market price of which is less than the amount of drawback due thereon, and Section 76(2) provides that no drawback shall be paid where the claim is less than ₹50. (Source: Section 76 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Prohibition of Drawback

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Rule 96 of the CGST Rules, 2017, how is the refund of IGST paid on export of goods processed?
options: The exporter must submit a physical manual claim to the jurisdictional GST Range Officer within ₹5 days
Refund is issued as physical promissory notes by the Reserve Bank of India
Refund is allowed only if no GST return is ever revised
The Shipping Bill filed by the exporter is itself deemed to be an application for refund once the Departure Manifest/EGM and GSTR-3B/GSTR-1 are filed, processed automatically via ICEGATE
explain: Rule 96 provides that the Shipping Bill having an IGST payment declaration is deemed to be a refund application. ICEGATE automatically validates the data with GSTN (Table 6A of GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B) and credits the refund directly via PFMS. (Source: Rule 96 CGST Rules / CBIC Circular 43/2017-Cus)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Rule 96 of CGST Rules, 2017

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: In the automated processing of IGST refunds on export of goods on ICEGATE, what does the frequent error code "SB005" signify?
options: Failure to obtain FSSAI license for engineering goods
Exporter's bank account is in an unapproved overseas bank
Invoice number, date, and port code mismatch between the Shipping Bill data on ICEGATE and Table 6A of GSTR-1 on the GST portal
explain: Error SB005 represents an invoice mismatch: the invoice number, date, or port code declared in the Shipping Bill does not match the details uploaded in Table 6A of GSTR-1, preventing automated clearance of IGST refund. (Source: CBIC Advisory on IGST Refund / ICEGATE)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — ICEGATE Error Code SB005

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: What is the crucial statutory difference between Section ₹3 (Pilferage) and Section 23 (Lost or Destroyed Goods) of the Customs Act, 1962 ?
options: Section ₹3 requires prior FIR registration; Section 23 requires a certificate from the President of India
Section ₹3 applies to warehoused goods; Section 23 does not
Section ₹3 applies only to exports; Section 23 applies only to imports

Under Section ₹3 , duty is not payable if goods are pilfered before clearance/warehousing order; under Section 23, duty is remitted on goods lost (other than pilferage) or destroyed before clearance for home consumption
explain: Under Section ₹3 , the importer is automatically not liable to pay duty if goods are pilfered before clearance for home consumption or warehousing (and custodian pays under Sec 45(3)). Section 23 covers non-pilferage losses and destruction (e.g. fire, acts of God) at any time before home consumption clearance. (Source: Section ₹3 & 23 Customs Act, 1962 / R.K. Jain)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 13 vs Section 23

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance (GFA) for an Indian resident or tourist of Indian origin arriving by air from any country other than Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar?
explain: Under Rule 3, an Indian resident or foreigner residing in India or a tourist of Indian origin arriving from countries other than Nepal, Bhutan or Myanmar is allowed clearance free of duty for articles up to an aggregate value of ₹50,000 (excluding Annexure I goods). Foreign tourists get Rs ₹5,000 . (Source: Rule 3 Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 — General Free Allowance (GFA)

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
section: Rule 4 — Arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar
text: Under Rule 4 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance for a passenger arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar across land borders versus arriving by air?
explain: Under Rule 4, passengers arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar by land borders have a GFA of Nil (only used personal effects are free). If arriving by air, the GFA is Rs ₹5,000 . (Source: Rule 4 Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 4 — Arriving from Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Rule 6 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what are the weight and value limitations for duty-free clearance of gold jewelry brought by an Indian passenger who has resided abroad for more than one year?
options: Gentlemen: Up to 20 grams with value cap of ₹50,000; Ladies: Up to 40 grams with value cap of ₹1,00,000
Gold jewelry is completely exempt with zero weight limit
explain: Rule 6 provides that a passenger residing abroad for over one year may bring duty-free jewelry in bona fide baggage: gentleman passenger up to 20 grams (value ceiling ₹50,000); lady passenger up to 40 grams (value ceiling ₹1,00,000). (Source: Rule 6 Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 6 — Jewelry Allowance

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Which of the following items is included in Annexure I of the Baggage Rules, 2016 (and is therefore strictly EXCLUDED from the General Free Allowance and always dutiable)?
explain: Annexure I includes: Firearms, cartridges > 50, cigarettes > ₹00 , cigars > 25, tobacco > 125g, alcohol/wine > 2 litres, gold/silver other than ornaments, and Flat Panel (LCD/LED/Plasma) TVs. These can never be cleared under the GFA. (Source: Annexure I Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Annexure I — Excluded Articles

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: What is the standard effective rate of customs duty charged on dutiable passenger baggage under Heading 9803 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 ?
options: 35% Basic Customs Duty + ₹0 % Social Welfare Surcharge (effective 38.5%)
Flat 50% ad valorem with zero cesses
explain: Baggage under Heading 9803 attracts a statutory BCD rate of 35%, along with a ₹0 % Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) on duty, resulting in an effective customs duty rate of 38.5%. (Source: Customs Tariff Heading 9803 / Notification 26/2016-Cus)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Duty Rate on Dutiable Baggage

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the default legal principle regarding goods produced or manufactured in India that are exported and subsequently re-imported?
options: They are liable to customs duty and subject to conditions/restrictions as if they were imported for the first time, unless exempted by notification
They can enter only under a Special Economic Zone permit
They can only be imported via parcel post
They are permanently exempt from all taxes because they originated in India
explain: Section 20 states that goods produced/manufactured in India, when re-imported, shall be liable to customs duty and subject to conditions as if imported for the first time, save as otherwise provided by Central Government exemption notifications (e.g. Notif 45/2017-Cus). (Source: Section 20 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Re-Importation of Indian Goods

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs, when Indian goods are exported for repair or alteration abroad and re-imported within 3 years, what is the customs duty liability on re-import?
options: Full customs duty on the entire value of the machinery as if newly purchased
Customs duty is payable only on the fair cost of repairs/alterations, cost of materials added, and two-way international freight and insurance
Completely free of all duties and GST without assessment
explain: Under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs, goods exported for repairs/alterations and re-imported within 3 years pay customs duty only on the value of repairs, materials added, and freight + insurance both ways, provided the goods are identified as the same. (Source: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Re-Import After Repairs Abroad

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
section: Re-Import of Goods Exported Under Drawback / IGST Refund
text: When goods exported under claim of duty drawback or IGST refund are re-imported into India within 3 years (e.g. due to rejection by foreign buyer), what is the condition for clearance under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs?
options: The importer must repay the amount of duty drawback or IGST refund availed at the time of export
The goods must be auctioned by the custodian
The importer must surrender his IEC to DGFT
The goods can only be released after 1 year in a bonded warehouse
explain: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs provides that when exported goods are returned due to rejection or lack of demand within 3 years, they are exempt from basic customs duty subject to repayment of the drawback availed or refund of IGST claimed at export. (Source: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs / CBIC Circular)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Re-Import of Goods Exported Under Drawback / IGST Refund

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015, what is the statutory time period within which the full export value of goods must be realized and repatriated to India?
options: 3 years from the date of realization of the bill of lading
9 months from the date of export (₹5 months if goods are exported to an overseas warehouse established with RBI approval)
₹80 days from the date of the commercial invoice
90 days from the date of Shipping Bill
explain: Under Regulation 9 of the FEMA (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations 2015 as amended by RBI, the realization period is 9 months from the date of export (₹5 months in case of goods exported to an approved warehouse abroad). (Source: RBI Master Direction on Export of Goods / FEMA ₹999 )
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Export Realisation & Repatriation Period

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: What are "EDPMS" and "IDPMS" deployed by the Reserve Bank of India in coordination with Customs?
options: Private software for calculating freight forwarding commissions

Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS) and Import Data Processing and Monitoring System (IDPMS) for tracking export realization and import outward remittances against Customs declarations
Maritime security tracking systems operated by the Indian Navy
Electronic systems for inspecting container seals
explain: EDPMS and IDPMS are RBI IT platforms integrating Customs Shipping Bills and Bills of Entry with Authorized Dealer banks to monitor real-time realization of export proceeds (e-BRC) and settlement of import remittances. (Source: RBI Master Directions / ICEGATE)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — EDPMS and IDPMS Systems

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under FEMA regulations, an arriving passenger entering India must submit a Currency Declaration Form (CDF) to Customs when bringing in foreign currency notes exceeding which thresholds?
options: When aggregate value of foreign currency notes exceeds USD 5,000 or aggregate value of currency notes plus travellers cheques exceeds USD ₹0,000
Declaration is optional irrespective of amount
explain: Under FEMA (Manner of Receipt and Payment) Regulations, a passenger must declare foreign exchange on a CDF if foreign currency bank notes exceed USD 5,000 or total foreign currency (notes + travellers cheques) exceeds USD ₹0,000 (or equivalent). (Source: RBI Master Direction / Customs Baggage Guide)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Foreign Currency Declaration (CDF)

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under RBI FEMA regulations, what is the maximum amount of Indian currency notes that an Indian resident may carry when travelling outside India (other than to Nepal or Bhutan)?
explain: Under Regulation 8 of FEMA (Export and Import of Currency) Regulations, an Indian resident travelling abroad (other than Nepal and Bhutan) may carry Indian currency notes up to a maximum of ₹25,000 per person. (Source: RBI Notification No. FEMA 6(R)/RB-2015)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Carriage of Indian Currency Notes

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under Rule 6 of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, which of the following declarations is MANDATORY on all imported pre-packaged commodities sold in India?
options: Name and address of manufacturer and importer, generic name, net quantity, month/year of manufacture/import, MRP (inclusive of all taxes in INR), and consumer care details
Only the country of origin in French or English
Only the barcode and foreign factory address
explain: Rule 6 of Legal Metrology (PC) Rules mandates: (1) Name & address of manufacturer/importer, (2) Common/generic name, (3) Net quantity, (4) Month & year of mfg/import, (5) Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and (6) Consumer care details. (Source: Legal Metrology (PC) Rules, 2011 / Ministry of Consumer Affairs)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 6 — Mandatory Declarations

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: If imported pre-packaged goods arrive without the mandatory Legal Metrology declarations, what customs relief is available under DGFT Notification No. 44/2000-Customs?
options: The importer is issued a non-bailable arrest warrant
The cargo must be destroyed immediately without notice
Goods are allowed for home consumption if the broker gives a verbal undertaking
The goods may be deposited in a customs bonded warehouse under Section 49 / Section 58, and mandatory labels affixed prior to clearance for home consumption
explain: Under DGFT Notification No. 44/2000-Cus read with CBIC Circulars, imported pre-packaged goods can be moved into a bonded warehouse where labeling/stickering of MRP and mandatory declarations can be completed prior to clearance for home consumption. (Source: DGFT Notif 44/2000-Cus / CBIC Circular No. ₹9 /2011-Cus)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Labeling in Bonded Warehouses

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017, what is the mandatory minimum remaining shelf life of imported food products at the time of customs clearance?
options: At least 90 days regardless of total shelf life
At least 25% of total shelf life
Not less than 60% of the total original shelf life of the product at the time of import clearance
explain: Regulation 5(6) of FSSAI (Import) Regulations, 2017 provides that Customs shall not clear any imported food item unless it has a valid shelf life of not less than 60% of its original total shelf life at the time of import. (Source: FSSAI (Import) Regulations, 2017 / CBIC SWIFT)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Shelf Life Requirement at Import

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: How is food safety import clearance obtained for food consignments entering India through Customs?
options: By visiting FSSAI headquarters in New Delhi with a sample

Through the ICEGATE SWIFT (Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade) portal, where FSSAI Authorised Officer conducts document verification, visual inspection, laboratory testing, and issues an online No Objection Certificate (NOC)
Food items do not require any FSSAI clearance if imported by air
By obtaining clearance from local municipal food inspectors at the dock
explain: Under the Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade (SWIFT) on ICEGATE, food import entries are automatically routed to the FSSAI Food Import Clearance System (FICS). An Authorised Officer (AO) samples, tests, and issues an electronic NOC or Non-Conformance Certificate (NCC). (Source: FSSAI Import Regulations 2017 / CBIC SWIFT Guidelines)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Import Clearance & SWIFT Interface

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 5 of CBLR, 2018, what is the minimum educational qualification generally prescribed for an individual applicant to appear for the Regulation 6 examination?
options: Postgraduate degree in Maritime Law exclusively
explain: Regulation 5(1) prescribes graduation from a recognised university as a fundamental educational qualification for an applicant appearing for the examination under Regulation 6. (Source: Regulation 5 CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (n) of CBLR, 2018, how must a Customs Broker verify the correctness of the Importer Exporter Code (IEC), GSTIN, identity, and address of the client?
options: Only through a self-declaration letter signed by the client
Only through a police verification certificate
Any one document chosen at the broker's discretion
Using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information, not being documents furnished by the client himself
explain: Regulation ₹0 (n) mandates that the Customs Broker must verify the identity and address of the client using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information, not merely documents furnished by the client himself. (Source: Regulation ₹0 (n) CBLR, 2018 / KYC Guidelines)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 17 (5) of CBLR, 2018, within what time period must the Inquiry Officer appointed by the Commissioner submit his inquiry report?
options: 90 days from the date of issue of the notice
₹80 days from the date of alleged contravention
30 days from the date of appointment
explain: Regulation 17 (5) mandates that the Inquiry Officer must complete the inquiry and submit his report within 90 days from the date of issue of the notice under Regulation 17 (1). (Source: Regulation 17 (5) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 17

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
text: Under the three-tier AEO Programme for importers and exporters notified by CBIC, which tier is granted solely on the basis of desktop verification without physical on-site verification?
explain: Under Circular No. 33/2016-Customs, AEO-T1 status is granted solely based on desktop verification of documentary compliance and clean fiscal history; physical site verification is not required. (Source: CBIC Circular 33/2016-Cus / AEO Guidelines)
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Circular No. 33/2016-Customs

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
section: AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 Bank Guarantee Benefits
text: What is the percentage waiver on furnishing Bank Guarantees granted to an entity holding AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 status under customs duty exemption and facilitation schemes?
explain: Under the AEO Programme, AEO-T2 holders are granted a 50% waiver on bank guarantee requirements, while AEO-T3 holders enjoy a ₹00 % waiver of bank guarantee under all duty exemption and remission schemes. (Source: Circular 33/2016-Customs)
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 Bank Guarantee Benefits

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
text: Which of the following supply chain actors is eligible to apply for AEO-LO (Logistics Operator) certification?
options: Customs Brokers, Logistics Providers, Custodians / Terminal Operators, and Warehouse Operators
Foreign manufacturers having no presence in India
Only software consultants developing EDI formats
explain: AEO-LO is specifically designed for intermediate supply chain entities including Customs Brokers, Logistics Providers, Custodians or Terminal Operators, and Warehouse Operators. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 33/2016-Customs)
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — AEO-LO Eligibility

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
text: What is the statutory certificate validity period for AEO-T1, AEO-T2, and AEO-T3 holders respectively under the Indian AEO Programme?
options: All tiers are valid for ₹0 years
AEO-T1: 5 years; AEO-T2: 5 years; AEO-T3: Permanent
AEO-T1: 3 years; AEO-T2: 3 years; AEO-T3: 5 years
AEO-T1: 1 year; AEO-T2: 2 years; AEO-T3: 3 years
explain: Under CBIC AEO guidelines, AEO-T1 and AEO-T2 certifications are valid for 3 years, while AEO-T3 and AEO-LO certifications are valid for 5 years, subject to continuous compliance. (Source: CBIC Circular 33/2016-Cus)
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Validity of AEO Certificates

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Section 28DA of the Customs Act, 1962 read with CAROTAR, 2020, what is the primary legal responsibility placed on an importer claiming preferential tariff treatment under a Free Trade Agreement (FTA)?
options: The importer must pay a mandatory origin verification tax of 5%
The importer must obtain written consent from the State Government
The importer must exercise origin due diligence, possess sufficient information to satisfy origin criteria (Form I), and cannot rely blindly on the Certificate of Origin
The importer has zero responsibility once a Certificate of Origin (COO) is issued
