explain: Section 28DA and Rule 3 of CAROTAR 2020 mandate that an importer claiming preferential tariff must exercise due diligence, possess origin-related information as outlined in Form I, and be satisfied that the goods meet origin criteria. (Source: Section 28DA Customs Act / CAROTAR 2020)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 28DA / Rule 3

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
section: Rule 5 - Time Limit to Furnish Information
text: Under Rule 5(1) of CAROTAR, 2020, when the proper officer raises a requisition for origin-related information or documents, within what time period must the importer furnish the required details?
explain: Rule 5(1) of CAROTAR 2020 requires the importer to provide the requisitioned origin information and supporting documents within ₹0 working days from the date of receipt of the requisition from the proper officer. (Source: Rule 5 CAROTAR 2020)
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Rule 5 - Time Limit to Furnish Information

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
text: Under Rule 6 of CAROTAR, 2020, who conducts retroactive verification of origin with the Issuing Authority of the exporting country?
options: The private shipping line carrying the goods
The designated Nodal Officer through the CBIC FTA Cell
The Indian High Commission directly without customs involvement
Any Appraiser on duty at the dock
explain: Rule 6 specifies that verification requests to the verification authority of the exporting country shall be sent by the designated Nodal Officer through the CBIC Trade / FTA Cell. (Source: Rule 6 CAROTAR 2020 / CBIC Circular 38/2020-Cus)
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Rule 6 - Verification from Exporting Country

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Rule 4 of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, what identifier is generated on the Common Portal upon submitting prior one-time intimation?
explain: Rule 4 of IGCR Rules 2022 provides that upon submitting one-time prior information on the common portal (ICEGATE), an IGCR Identification Number (IIN) is automatically generated. (Source: Rule 4 IGCR Rules, 2022)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 4 - One-Time Intimation & IIN

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Rule 6 of the IGCR Rules, 2022, by which day of the succeeding month must the importer submit an electronic monthly statement on the Common Portal detailing the receipt and consumption of concessional duty goods?
explain: Rule 6 of IGCR Rules 2022 requires the importer to submit a monthly statement on the common portal by the tenth day of the following month, accounting for all goods received and consumed. (Source: Rule 6 IGCR Rules, 2022)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 6 - Monthly Statement

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
section: Rule 7 & 8 - Job Work of Concessional Goods
text: Under the IGCR Rules, 2022, what is the maximum time limit within which goods sent for job work from the importer's manufacturing premises must be received back?
options: 6 months from the date of sending the goods (extendable by the jurisdictional officer)
explain: Rule 7(3) of IGCR Rules 2022 mandates that goods sent for job work shall be received back within a period of six months from the date of dispatch, subject to extension by the jurisdictional officer. (Source: Rule 7 IGCR Rules, 2022)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 7 & 8 - Job Work of Concessional Goods

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 28H of the Customs Act, 1962 , on which of the following questions can an eligible applicant seek an Advance Ruling from the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR)?
options: On whether the customs duty can be waived completely on political grounds
Only on the personal income tax slab of the importer
Classification of goods, applicability of exemption notifications, and principles of valuation under Section ₹4
explain: Section 28H(2) permits advance rulings on: (a) classification of goods, (b) applicability of exemption notifications, (c) valuation principles under Section ₹4 , and (d) origin determination under trade agreements. (Source: Section 28H Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 28H

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 28-I(6) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR) is required to pronounce its advance ruling within what time limit from the date of receipt of the application?
explain: Section 28-I(6) provides that the Authority shall pronounce its advance ruling in writing within three months from the date of receipt of the application. (Source: Section 28-I(6) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 28-I

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 28J of the Customs Act, 1962 , an advance ruling pronounced by CAAR is binding on:
options: Only the applicant who sought it and in respect of the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs and his subordinate officers
All foreign shipping lines operating in Indian waters
All importers across India indiscriminately as a general law
explain: Section 28J(1) specifies that an advance ruling shall be binding only on the applicant who sought it and on the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs in respect of the concerned transaction. (Source: Section 28J Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 28J

chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
text: Under Section 99A of the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, what are the two statutory forms of customs audit conducted by the department?
options: RBI Currency Audit and DGFT Quota Audit
Police Investigation Audit and Municipal Audit
Transaction Based Audit (TBA) and Premises Based Audit (PBA)
Pre-shipment Audit and Port Trust Audit
explain: Section 99A read with Customs Audit Regulations 2018 recognizes Transaction Based Audit (TBA) at customs stations and Premises Based Audit (PBA) conducted at the registered commercial premises of the auditee. (Source: Section 99A Customs Act / Customs Audit Regs 2018)
topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Section 99A / Customs Audit Regulations, 2018

chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
text: Under Regulation 4 of the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, for what minimum period must an auditee preserve all customs declarations, invoices, and accounting records relevant to imported/export goods?
options: 5 years from the date of clearance of goods
explain: Regulation 4 requires every auditee to maintain and preserve books of accounts, records, documents and customs declarations for a period of not less than 5 years from the date of clearance of the goods. (Source: Regulation 4 Customs Audit Regulations, 2018)
topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Regulation 4 - Preservation of Records

chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
text: Under the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, what advance intimation notice must ordinarily be served on an auditee prior to conducting a Premises Based Audit (PBA)?
options: At least ₹5 days advance notice in writing
No notice is required; surprise visits are mandatory
explain: Regulation 5 mandates that the proper officer shall give an advance notice in writing of at least ₹5 days to the auditee before conducting an audit at their premises. (Source: Regulation 5 Customs Audit Regulations, 2018)
topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Notice for Premises Based Audit

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (HCCAR), what is the statutory status of an entity appointed to handle and store imported goods in a customs area?
options: Sole Agent of the Ministry of Commerce
Customs Cargo Services Provider (CCSP) / Custodian under Section 45
explain: Under HCCAR 2009, persons handling imported or export goods in customs areas are designated as Customs Cargo Services Providers (CCSPs) and operate as Custodians under Section 45 of the Customs Act. (Source: HCCAR 2009 / Section 45)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5 & Section 45

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Regulation 5(1)(h) of HCCAR, 2009, a Customs Cargo Services Provider (CCSP) must install high-definition CCTV systems and preserve the recorded video footage for a minimum period of:
explain: Regulation 5(1)(h) of HCCAR 2009 mandates that CCSPs must maintain 24x7 CCTV coverage of all cargo handling, entry, and exit points and preserve the video recordings for a minimum of 30 days for inspection by customs. (Source: Regulation 5(1)(h) HCCAR 2009)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — CCTV Video Footage Retention

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under the revised SVB guidelines issued vide CBIC Circular No. 05/2016-Customs, which transactions are investigated by the Special Valuation Branch?
options: Only imports of gold bullion by scheduled banks
Imports between related persons under Rule 2(2) of CVR 2007 where relationship may have influenced price, and cases involving royalties, license fees or subsequent resale proceeds
All imports exceeding Rs ₹0 Crores in value
All shipments arriving from neighboring land border countries
explain: Circular No. 05/2016-Customs provides that SVBs investigate cases where buyer and seller are related under Rule 2(2) of CVR 2007 and there is prima facie ground to believe the relationship influenced invoice price, or where royalty/license fees/assists are involved. (Source: Circular 05/2016-Customs)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Circular No. 05/2016-Customs

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: What is the general policy regarding Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) during the pendency of an SVB investigation under Circular No. 05/2016-Customs?
options: Zero EDD is collected as a matter of standard practice; 1% EDD is levied only if the importer fails to submit the prescribed Annexure/information within 60 days
EDD equal to ₹00 % of the Basic Customs Duty
Compulsory ₹0 % cash deposit with the Reserve Bank of India
Compulsory 5% EDD in every related party transaction
explain: Under the revamped SVB procedure, the practice of routinely imposing Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) was abolished. EDD @ 1% is imposed only if the importer fails to submit the completed questionnaire/documents within 60 days of requisition. (Source: CBIC Circular No. 05/2016-Customs)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) Policy

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Heading 9801 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 read with Project Imports Regulations, ₹986 , what is the core commercial benefit of registering an industrial project under the Project Import scheme?
options: Exemption from filing a Bill of Entry
All project goods, machinery, and accompanying spare parts are assessed at a single uniform customs duty rate instead of separate itemized classifications under multiple tariff chapters
Complete exemption from IGST without condition
explain: Project Imports scheme under Heading 9801 provides a single, uniform concessional rate of basic customs duty for all items, machinery, and initial spare parts imported for setting up a new plant or undertaking substantial expansion. (Source: Project Imports Regulations, ₹986 / )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Heading 9801 Scope

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Regulation 7 of the Project Imports Regulations, ₹986 , within what time period after plant commissioning must the importer submit a plant completion certificate and reconciliation statement for finalization of contract?
explain: Regulation 7 requires the importer to submit a plant completion and commissioning certificate from a Chartered Engineer or sponsoring authority along with final reconciliation within three months (extendable up to six months by the Commissioner). (Source: Regulation 7 Project Imports Regulations, ₹986 )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Plant Commissioning & Contract Finalization

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010, which electronic declaration form is filed for commercial import cargo of high value?
explain: Under Courier Regulations 2010: CBE-XI is for documents, CBE-XII is for free gifts/samples up to Rs ₹0,000 , CBE-XIII is for low value dutiable, CBE-XIV is for medium value, and CBE-XV is for commercial high-value goods. (Source: Courier Regulations, 2010 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Electronic Declaration Forms

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Which of the following commodities is completely prohibited from being imported or exported through courier mode under customs regulations?
options: Precious stones, gold or silver in bullion, arms and ammunition, and live animals
explain: Regulation 2(2) strictly prohibits the carriage of precious or semi-precious stones, gold or silver bullion, arms, ammunition, explosives, livestock, animals, plants, and narcotic substances via courier mode. (Source: Courier Imports and Exports Regulations, 2010)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Prohibited Cargo by Courier

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 127B of the Customs Act, 1962 , which of the following is a mandatory prerequisite for an applicant to file an application before the Customs Settlement Commission?
options: The additional amount of customs duty accepted by the applicant in the application must exceed ₹3 Lakhs, and the applicant must have filed a Bill of Entry/Shipping Bill and received an SCN
The applicant must deposit ₹00 % penalty before applying
The applicant must have already been convicted by a criminal court
The case must involve contraband gold seized on person
explain: Section 127B mandates that the applicant must have filed a Bill of Entry/Shipping Bill, received a Show Cause Notice, made full and true disclosure, admitted additional duty liability exceeding ₹3 Lakhs, and paid such duty with interest. (Source: Section 127B Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 127B - Eligibility Criteria

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: What statutory immunity can the Customs Settlement Commission grant under Section 127H of the Customs Act, 1962 upon being satisfied with full cooperation by the applicant?
options: Immunity from complying with FSSAI regulations
Immunity from GST audits for ₹0 years
Immunity from prosecution for any offence under the Customs Act or IPC in relation to the case, and immunity from whole or part of any penalty and fine
Immunity from payment of Basic Customs Duty
explain: Section 127H empowers the Settlement Commission to grant immunity from prosecution for any offence under the Customs Act or Indian Penal Code, as well as from the imposition of whole or any part of penalties and fines. (Source: Section 127H Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 127H - Power to Grant Immunity

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
section: Section 30 of SEZ Act - DTA Sales
text: Under Section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, when goods manufactured or produced in an SEZ are cleared into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), customs duty is chargeable at what rate?
options: At the internal state VAT rate only
Completely free of all customs duty since manufacture occurred within India
At the rates of customs duties, including BCD and IGST, as are leviable on import of such goods into India from outside India
explain: Section 30 of the SEZ Act provides that any goods removed or cleared from an SEZ into the DTA shall be chargeable to customs duty, including anti-dumping, countervailing, and safeguard duties, as are leviable on such goods when imported into India. (Source: Section 30 SEZ Act, 2005)
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 30 of SEZ Act - DTA Sales

chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
text: Under the Sea Cargo Manifest and Transhipment Regulations, 2018 (SCMTR), what is a 'PCIN' (Pre-Cargo Information Number)?
options: A unique identifier generated by ICEGATE upon submission of cargo details by the freight forwarder / cargo aggregator before vessel departure from origin port
A port parking slot booking number
A vessel tracking transponder frequency code
A customs officer's digital signature key
explain: Under SCMTR 2018, PCIN is the Pre-Cargo Information Number generated by the customs system when cargo details are filed electronically by the consignor/freight forwarder prior to departure of the vessel from the load port. (Source: SCMTR 2018 / CBIC Guidelines)
topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Sea Arrival Manifest (SAM) & PCIN

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: How is assessable value determined for customs clearance of imported goods purchased on a High Sea Sale (HSS) basis?
options: By deducting ocean freight from the purchase invoice
Always by adding flat ₹0 % HSS commission to original invoice
Always on the original manufacturer invoice only, ignoring the HSS contract price

On the basis of the actual High Sea Sale contract price paid by the final high sea buyer (which includes original CIF value plus high sea sale margin/profit), provided it reflects genuine commercial transaction value
explain: Under Section ₹4 and CBIC instructions, assessable value for HSS transactions is the actual price paid by the high sea buyer to the high sea seller (inclusive of HSS margin/profit), reflecting the price at the time and place of importation. (Source: CBIC Circulars / R.K. Jain)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Valuation of High Sea Sales

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the IPR (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules, 2007, when Customs suspends clearance of suspected counterfeit goods upon notice by the right holder, within what time period must the right holder join proceedings and execute the requisite bond and bank guarantee?
options: ₹0 working days (3 working days in case of perishable goods)
explain: Rule 7(1) of IPR Rules 2007 mandates that the right holder must join proceedings within ₹0 working days (or 3 working days for perishable goods) of being notified of suspension of clearance, failing which the goods shall be released. (Source: Rule 7 IPR Rules, 2007)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 5 & Rule 7 - Suspension of Clearance

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under Rule 9 of the IPR (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules, 2007, how must confiscated counterfeit trademark goods be treated?
options: They must be gifted to customs officers
They can be re-exported in their original state to the manufacturer
They shall be destroyed or disposed of outside the channels of commerce, and cannot be allowed to be re-exported in an unaltered state
They must be sold through customs public auction after removing outer cartons only
explain: Rule 9 prohibits allowing confiscated counterfeit goods to be re-exported in an unaltered state; they must be destroyed under customs supervision or disposed of outside commercial channels with right holder concurrence. (Source: Rule 9 IPR Rules, 2007)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Disposal of Confiscated Counterfeit Goods

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under the Foreign Trade Policy conditions for import of brand-new passenger cars, which of the following is a mandatory technical and homologation compliance requirement?
options: No homologation is required if imported by air
The vehicle must be left-hand drive
The vehicle must have an engine capacity exceeding 5000cc exclusively
The vehicle must have right-hand steering, speedometer calibrated in km/h, and a homologation road-worthiness certificate issued by ARAI/VRDE/ICAT
explain: Policy Conditions mandate that new imported vehicles must be right-hand drive, have speedometers in km/h, meet photometric and emissions standards, and submit a type-approval certificate from designated testing agencies like ARAI or ICAT. (Source: ITC(HS) Policy)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Policy Condition 1 of Chapter 87

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: What is the statutory requirement for import of un-shredded metallic waste and scrap into India under the Foreign Trade Policy?
options: It requires a Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificate (PSIC) from a DGFT-approved agency certifying that the consignment contains no arms, ammunition, mines, or radiation, and must enter through designated ports equipped with Radiation Portal Monitors
Import of metallic scrap is completely banned in India
It requires approval from the Reserve Bank of India
It can enter through any small land customs station without inspection
explain: Paragraph 2.54 of HBP mandates that un-shredded scrap must be accompanied by a PSIC from an approved inspection agency certifying absence of explosives, shells, and radioactive contamination, and can clear only through designated ports with portal radiation monitors. (Source: FTP 2023 HBP Para 2.54)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificate (PSIC)

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹23 of the Customs Act, 1962 , when specified goods (such as gold, bullion, watches, diamonds, synthetic yarn, cigarettes) are seized in the reasonable belief that they are smuggled goods, on whom does the burden of proving that they are NOT smuggled goods rest?
options: On the manufacturer in the foreign country
On the person from whose possession the goods were seized, or any person who claims to be the owner thereof
Strictly on the Customs Appraising Officer who seized them
explain: Section ₹23 is a statutory exception to normal criminal jurisprudence: the burden of proving that the seized goods are not smuggled goods lies squarely on the person from whose possession they were seized. (Source: Section ₹23 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 123 - Burden of Proof

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹02 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , when an officer is about to search any person under Section ₹00 or ₹01 , what mandatory right must the officer inform the person of?
options: The right to refuse search unconditionally
The right to be taken without unnecessary delay before the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate
The right to immediate legal representation before the Supreme Court
The right to claim cash compensation on the spot
explain: Section ₹02 (1) mandates that the officer about to search a person shall inform him that he has the right to be taken before the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate. (Source: Section ₹02 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 102 - Search of Persons

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹10 (2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , where goods are seized by customs and no Show Cause Notice is given under Section ₹24 within what time period (extendable by up to 6 months by Principal Commissioner), must the seized goods be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized?
options: 6 months from the date of seizure
explain: Section ₹10 (2) provides that where any goods are seized and no notice under Section ₹24 (a) is given within six months (or extended six months by Principal Commissioner upon sufficient cause), the goods shall be returned to the person from whom seized. (Source: Section ₹10 (2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110(2) - Seizure Notice Timeline

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section 110A of the Customs Act, 1962 , how may any goods, documents or conveyances seized under Section ₹10 be provisionally released to the owner pending adjudication?
options: By obtaining an order from the local municipal panchayat
Only upon payment of full redemption fine in cash upfront
Provisional release is prohibited under Indian law
Upon execution by the owner of a bond with such security or bank guarantee as the adjudicating authority may require
explain: Section 110A empowers the adjudicating authority to release seized goods, documents, or conveyances provisionally to the owner on taking a bond in the proper form with appropriate security/bank guarantee. (Source: Section 110A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110A - Provisional Release

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹15 (2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , when is a conveyance (truck, vessel, aircraft) used in the smuggling of goods NOT liable to confiscation?
options: If the conveyance is owned by a foreign company
If the owner proves that it was so used without the knowledge or connivance of the owner himself, his agent, and the person-in-charge, and each of them had taken all reasonable precautions
If the cargo value is less than the truck value
If the driver was driving below the speed limit
explain: Section ₹15 (2) provides that a conveyance shall not be confiscated if the owner proves that it was used without knowledge or connivance of the owner, agent, or master, and that all reasonable precautions had been taken. (Source: Section ₹15 (2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 115 - Confiscation of Conveyances

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
section: Section 121 - Sale Proceeds of Smuggled Goods
text: Under Section ₹21 of the Customs Act, 1962 , where any smuggled goods are sold by a person having knowledge or reason to believe that the goods are smuggled goods, what can customs confiscate?
options: Nothing, once the goods have changed hands
explain: Section ₹21 provides that where any smuggled goods are sold by a person with knowledge or reason to believe they are smuggled, the sale-proceeds thereof shall be liable to confiscation. (Source: Section ₹21 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 121 - Sale Proceeds of Smuggled Goods

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Section ₹49 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the crucial legal restriction on amending a Bill of Entry or Shipping Bill AFTER the goods have been cleared for home consumption or for export?
options: No amendment shall be allowed except on the basis of documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited, or exported
No amendment is ever permitted under any circumstance
Amendments can be made only with prior permission of the Reserve Bank of India
Amendments can be made freely within 5 years without proof
explain: The proviso to Section ₹49 strictly bars any amendment of an entry after clearance, except on the basis of documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited, or exported. (Source: Section ₹49 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 149 - Amendment of Documents

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Which national online infrastructure operates as the notified 'Common Customs Electronic Portal' under Section 154C of the Customs Act, 1962 for filing registrations, declarations, and service of orders?
explain: Under Section 154C, the Central Government notified the ICEGATE portal (www.icegate.gov.in) as the Common Customs Electronic Portal for paperless processing, electronic declarations, and digital service of notices. (Source: Section 154C Customs Act / Notif 33/2021-Cus (N.T.))
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 154C - Common Customs Electronic Portal

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
section: Section 155 - Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith
text: What statutory protection does Section ₹55 of the Customs Act, 1962 afford to customs officers and Central Government personnel?
options: Absolute immunity from criminal law for any deliberate corruption
Automatic promotion upon completing five years of service
No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Government or any customs officer for anything done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act
explain: Section ₹55 (1) protects the Central Government and officers from civil suits or criminal prosecutions for acts done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of the Act or rules. (Source: Section ₹55 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 155 - Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
section: Regulation 13 - Form G & Form F Cards
text: Under Regulation 13 of CBLR, 2018, which identity card is issued to an employee/assistant of a Customs Broker who has passed the examination conducted under Regulation 13 (5)?
explain: Regulation 13 (5) provides that an employee who qualifies in the examination conducted by customs is issued a photo identity card in Form G, authorizing him to sign customs documents and transact business on behalf of the broker. (Source: Regulation 13 CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 13 - Form G & Form F Cards

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 18 of CBLR, 2018, what is the maximum financial penalty that the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs can impose on a Customs Broker for contravention of any provision of the regulations?
explain: Regulation 18 empowers the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs to impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees (₹50,000) on a Customs Broker for failure to comply with any provision of CBLR 2018. (Source: Regulation 18 CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 18 - Penalty on Customs Broker

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (f) of CBLR, 2018, for what minimum period is a Customs Broker statutorily required to maintain and preserve all records and accounts relating to customs transactions?
explain: Regulation ₹0 (f) mandates that a Customs Broker must maintain up to date all records, accounts and documents for a period of not less than five years, and produce them before the proper officer upon inspection. (Source: Regulation ₹0 (f) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(f)

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: What is the fundamental statutory difference between 'Transit' under Section 53 and 'Transhipment' under Section 54 of the Customs Act, 1962 ?
options: Transit requires payment of full customs duty; transhipment is exempt from all laws
Transit applies only to export goods; transhipment applies only to passenger baggage
Transit applies only to air cargo; transhipment applies only to railway wagons

In transit, goods remain on the same conveyance throughout until reaching the destination port; in transhipment, goods are transferred from one conveyance to another conveyance under a transhipment permit and bond without payment of duty
explain: Under Section 53 (Transit), cargo mentioned in the manifest for another port stays on the same vessel/aircraft. Under Section 54 (Transhipment), cargo is unloaded and transferred to another vessel/aircraft/truck under a transhipment permit and bond. (Source: Section 53 & 54 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 53 & Section 54

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, which of the following conditions must be satisfied for the transaction value to be accepted by the proper officer?
options: The buyer and seller must be related in all commercial transactions
The payment must be settled exclusively in cash at the port
The invoice value must be exactly identical to the Directorate of Valuation benchmark

There are no restrictions as to the disposition or use of the goods by the buyer, other than restrictions imposed by Indian law or public authorities, or limiting geographical resale area, or not substantially affecting value
explain: Rule 3(2) stipulates four mandatory conditions: (a) no restrictions on disposition/use (except statutory/territorial), (b) sale not subject to unascertainable condition, (c) no proceeds reversion without Rule ₹0 adjustment, and (d) buyer and seller are not related or price is acceptable under Rule 3(3). (Source: Rule 3(2) CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(2) - Conditions for Transaction Value

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what is a mandatory statutory test for goods to qualify as 'identical goods'?
options: They must be manufactured in any country in the world by any corporation
They must be the same in all respects, including physical characteristics, quality, and reputation, and produced in the same country by the same person (or another person if none available)
They must have been exported at least 5 years apart
They must merely belong to the same 2-digit tariff chapter
explain: Rule 2(1)(d) and Rule 4 define 'identical goods' as goods which are the same in all respects, including physical characteristics, quality, and reputation, produced in the same country by the same person who produced the goods being valued (or another producer if none from same producer). (Source: Rule 4 CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 4 - Identical Goods Method

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 5 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what defines 'similar goods' for customs appraisal purposes?
options: Goods which, although not alike in all respects, have like characteristics and like component materials which enable them to perform the same functions and to be commercially interchangeable, produced in the same country
Goods imported in the same shipping container
Goods carrying identical brand trademarks regardless of origin
Goods that look visually alike but have entirely different functions
explain: Rule 2(1)(f) and Rule 5 define 'similar goods' as goods which have like characteristics and component materials enabling them to perform the same functions and be commercially interchangeable, produced in the same country. (Source: Rule 5 CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 5 - Similar Goods Method

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 7 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007 (Deductive Value Method), what is the starting price point for determining assessable value?
options: The retail maximum selling price in the country of exportation

The unit price at which the imported goods (or identical/similar goods) are sold in the greatest aggregate quantity to persons who are not related to the sellers in India at or about the time of importation
The price declared on the shipping bill of previous exports
The replacement manufacturing cost estimated by customs appraisers
explain: Rule 7(1) provides that the value is based on the unit price at which imported goods or identical/similar imported goods are sold in India in the greatest aggregate quantity to unrelated buyers, subject to statutory deductions. (Source: Rule 7 CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 7 - Deductive Value Method

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007 (Computed Value Method), what components constitute the computed value?
options: The cost of materials and fabrication, plus an amount for profit and general expenses equal to that usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class by producers in the country of exportation, plus Rule ₹0 (2) costs
The retail price in India minus 50% flat discount
Only the freight and insurance paid for transit
The highest price recorded at the London Metal Exchange
explain: Rule 8 prescribes that computed value consists of: (a) cost or value of materials and fabrication, (b) profit and general expenses usually reflected in exports to India, and (c) transportation, loading, and insurance costs under Rule ₹0 (2). (Source: Rule 8 CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 8 - Computed Value Method

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 9 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007 (Residual Method), which of the following valuation bases is EXPRESSLY PROHIBITED from being adopted?
options: Data available from previous genuine imports of similar goods
The selling price in India of goods produced in India, the price of goods in the domestic market of the exporting country, or arbitrary/fictitious values
Reasonable means consistent with the principles of Section ₹4
explain: Rule 9(2) expressly prohibits: (a) selling price of Indian goods, (b) system where highest value is adopted, (c) domestic market price in country of export, (d) cost of production other than computed values, (e) price for export to a third country, (f) minimum customs values, or (g) arbitrary or fictitious values. (Source: Rule 9(2) CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 9 - Residual Method Prohibitions

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹0 (1)(a)(i) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, how are 'buying commissions' treated when calculating the customs transaction value?
options: Buying commissions are expressly excluded from being added to the price actually paid or payable
Buying commissions must be credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund
Buying commissions must be compulsorily added to invoice value at flat 5%
Buying commissions are subjected to full basic customs duty plus IGST separately
explain: Rule ₹0 (1)(a)(i) states that commissions and brokerage, except buying commissions, incurred by the buyer shall be added to the price paid or payable. Buying commission paid to an agent representing the buyer is not includible. (Source: Rule ₹0 (1)(a)(i) CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(1)(a) - Buying Commissions

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹0 (1)(b)(iv) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what is the statutory rule regarding the value of engineering, development, artwork, and design work supplied by the buyer?
options: The value of such engineering, development, artwork, and design work is includible in assessable value ONLY if undertaken outside India
All engineering and design work is includible regardless of where undertaken
Assists can only be valued if the supplier is a public sector undertaking
Development work undertaken in India must be taxed at double the value
explain: Rule ₹0 (1)(b)(iv) specifies that the value of engineering, development, artwork, design work, and plans and sketches is added only if undertaken elsewhere than in India and is necessary for the production of the imported goods. (Source: Rule ₹0 (1)(b)(iv) CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(1)(b) - Assists Undertaken in India

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
section: Rule 10(2) - Freight and Insurance Not Ascertainable
text: Under Rule ₹0 (2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, where the actual cost of transportation and the actual cost of insurance are not ascertainable, how are they computed?
options: Freight @ 5% of FOB; Insurance @ 0.5% of FOB
Freight @ 20% of FOB value; Insurance @ 1.₹25 % of FOB value
Freight @ ₹0 % of FOB; Insurance @ 2% of FOB
explain: Under the proviso to Rule ₹0 (2), if transportation cost is not ascertainable, it shall be 20% of FOB value. If insurance cost is not ascertainable, it shall be 1.₹25 % of FOB value. (Source: Rule ₹0 (2) CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) - Freight and Insurance Not Ascertainable

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under the third proviso to Rule ₹0 (2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what ceiling applies to the cost of transport for goods imported by air?
options: Air freight can never exceed ₹0 % of CIF value
There is no ceiling; actual air freight must always be added in full
Where goods are imported by air, the transportation cost added shall not exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods, even if actual air freight incurred is higher
Air freight is capped at Rs ₹00 per kilogram
explain: The proviso to Rule ₹0 (2)(a) specifically mandates that in the case of goods imported by air, the cost of transport, loading, unloading, and handling charges shall not exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods. (Source: Rule ₹0 (2) CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) - Air Freight Limitation

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹2 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, what procedure must the proper officer follow before rejecting the declared transaction value?
options: The officer can issue a confiscation order instantly without any explanation
The officer must demand 50% deposit before raising any query
The officer must have reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of declared value, intimate the grounds of doubt in writing, give reasonable opportunity of being heard, and record reasons for rejection
The officer must obtain approval from the Ministry of External Affairs
explain: Rule ₹2 mandates that where the proper officer has reason to doubt the truth or accuracy of declared value, he shall ask the importer for further information, intimate grounds of doubt, provide reasonable opportunity of being heard, and record reasons in writing. (Source: Rule ₹2 CVR, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 12 - Rejection of Declared Value

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 28(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the normal statutory time limit for the proper officer to serve a Show Cause Notice for non-levy, short-levy, or erroneous refund not involving collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
options: 2 years from the relevant date (amended from 1 year by Finance Act, 2016)
explain: Section 28(1)(a) provides that in normal cases not involving collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, the proper officer shall serve a notice within two years from the relevant date. (Source: Section 28(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(1) - Normal Limitation Period

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 28(4) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the extended limitation period to issue a Show Cause Notice where duty has not been levied or has been short-levied by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
explain: Section 28(4) provides an extended limitation period of five years from the relevant date where duty has not been levied, short-levied, or erroneously refunded by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts. (Source: Section 28(4) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(4) - Extended Limitation Period

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
section: Section 28(5) - Reduced Penalty on Early Payment
text: Under Section 28(5) of the Customs Act, 1962 , where a notice is issued under Section 28(4) (extended period) and the noticee pays the duty, interest, and penalty within 30 days of receipt of the notice, what is the concessional penalty payable?
options: 25% of the penalty specified in the notice
explain: Under Section 28(5), where any person to whom a notice is served under Section 28(4) pays the duty in full, interest under Section 28AA, and a penalty equal to ₹5 % of the duty within 30 days of receipt of the notice, proceedings in respect of such duty shall be deemed to be concluded. (Source: Section 28(5) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(5) - Reduced Penalty on Early Payment

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
section: Section 28AA - Interest on Delayed Payment of Duty
text: Under Section 28AA of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory rate of interest notified by the Central Government on delayed payment of customs duty?
explain: Under Section 28AA read with Notification No. 33/2016-Customs (N.T.), the Central Government has fixed the rate of interest on delayed payment of customs duty at ₹5 % per annum from the date specified under the Act till actual payment. (Source: Section 28AA / Notif 33/2016-Cus (N.T.))
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28AA - Interest on Delayed Payment of Duty

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 281B of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the initial statutory validity period of an order of provisional attachment of property passed to protect revenue during pendency of recovery proceedings?
options: 6 months (extendable by Principal Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing, total period not exceeding 2 years)
explain: Section 281B(2) provides that every order of provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of six months, subject to extension by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing up to a total maximum of two years. (Source: Section 281B Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 281B - Provisional Attachment

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹12 (a)(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the maximum penalty leviable on a person in case of improper importation of PROHIBITED goods?
options: Flat penalty equal to ₹0 % of CIF value
Penalty not exceeding the value of the goods or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater
Penalty not exceeding twice the ocean freight
explain: Section ₹12 (a)(i) provides that in the case of goods in respect of which any prohibition is in force under the Act or any other law, the penalty shall not exceed the value of the goods or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater. (Source: Section ₹12 (a)(i) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 112(a) - Penalty for Improper Importation

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹12 (a)(ii) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the maximum penalty in case of improper importation of dutiable goods (other than prohibited goods)?
options: Penalty not exceeding five times the market price
Penalty not exceeding ten percent of the duty sought to be evaded or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater
explain: Section ₹12 (a)(ii) provides that in the case of dutiable goods, other than prohibited goods, the penalty shall not exceed ten percent of the duty sought to be evaded or five thousand rupees, whichever is the greater. (Source: Section ₹12 (a)(ii) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 112(a)(ii) - Penalty for Dutiable Goods

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962 , where duty has not been levied or has been short-levied by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, what is the quantum of penalty determined?
options: Penalty equal to 50% of the FOB export value
No penalty is leviable if the person is a first-time importer
A mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest so determined (reduced to 25% if duty, interest, and penalty are paid within 30 days of receipt of order)
explain: Section 114A imposes a mandatory penalty equal to the duty or interest determined under Section 28(8). The first proviso reduces this penalty to 25% if the duty, interest, and reduced penalty are paid within 30 days of the communication of the order. (Source: Section 114A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114A - Mandatory Penalty for Fraud

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section 114AA of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the maximum penalty leviable on a person who knowingly or intentionally makes, signs, or uses any false or incorrect declaration, statement, or document in the transaction of any customs business?
options: Penalty equal to 1% of the invoice value
Penalty not exceeding five times the value of goods
explain: Section 114AA prescribes that if a person knowingly or intentionally makes, signs, or uses any declaration, statement, or document which is false or incorrect in any material particular, he shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five times the value of goods. (Source: Section 114AA Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114AA - False Declarations and Invoices

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹17 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the maximum residual penalty for any person who contravenes any provision of the Act or fails to comply with any provision where no express penalty is elsewhere provided?
explain: Section ₹17 provides a general penalty for contraventions where no express penalty is provided in the Act, with a maximum ceiling of up to four lakh rupees (₹4,00,000), increased from ₹1,00,000 by Finance Act, 2019. (Source: Section ₹17 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 117 - General Penalty

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹25 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory ceiling on the fine that may be imposed in lieu of confiscation (Redemption Fine)?
options: The fine cannot exceed 50% of the assessable value
The redemption fine cannot exceed the CIF value of the goods
The fine shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable thereon
The fine is fixed at a flat ₹25,000 across all commodities
explain: The proviso to Section ₹25 (1) mandates that the redemption fine shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the customs duty chargeable thereon. (Source: Section ₹25 (1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 125 - Redemption Fine

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 58A of the Customs Act, 1962 , which category of goods is statutorily required to be deposited only in a 'Special Warehouse' under this section?
options: General iron and steel structural coils
Sensitive goods notified by the Board, including gold, silver, precious stones, duty-free shop goods, and ship stores/aircraft stores under physical customs lock
explain: Section 58A(1) read with the Special Warehouse Licensing Regulations, 2016 applies to sensitive goods notified by CBIC, such as gold, silver, duty-free shop merchandise, and ship/airline stores, requiring physical customs lock and control. (Source: Section 58A Customs Act / Notif 66/2016-Cus (N.T.))
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 58A - Special Warehouses

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 59(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , for what sum must the importer execute a warehousing bond before warehoused goods are allowed to be deposited in a warehouse?
options: A sum equal to the duty assessed
A sum equal to thrice (three times) the amount of the duty assessed on the goods
A sum equal to twice the amount of duty assessed
A sum equal to the total CIF value of the shipment
explain: Section 59(1) mandates that the importer shall execute a bond in a sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed on the goods, binding himself to observe all provisions and pay all duties, interest, and charges. (Source: Section 59(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 59 - Warehousing Bond Multiplier

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 61(1)(c) of the Customs Act, 1962 , for what period may general imported goods (other than capital goods or inputs for EOUs/MOOWR) remain warehoused in a warehouse?
options: One year from the date of the order made under Section 60 (extendable by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner for up to 1 year at a time)
explain: Section 61(1)(c) specifies that in the case of any other goods, they may remain in the warehouse till the expiry of one year from the date of the order permitting deposit under Section 60, subject to extension by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner. (Source: Section 61(1)(c) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 61(1) - Permissible Warehousing Period

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 61(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , where general warehoused goods remain in the warehouse beyond what initial period is interest payable on the customs duty till clearance?
options: After the expiry of ninety (90) days from the date of the order permitting deposit under Section 60
Interest is never charged on warehoused goods
explain: Section 61(2) provides that where any goods specified in Section 61(1)(c) remain in a warehouse beyond a period of ninety days, interest @ ₹5 % per annum shall be payable on the amount of duty from the expiry of the said ninety days till clearance. (Source: Section 61(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 61(2) - Interest on Warehoused Goods

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with MOOWR Regulations, 2019, what is the customs duty liability when goods manufactured in a bonded warehouse are cleared for export outside India?
options: No customs duty is payable on the imported raw materials or capital goods contained in or used for manufacturing the exported goods (duty remitted)
Full customs duty is payable on all raw materials and machinery
Duty must be paid and then claimed as drawback after 2 years
A flat export surcharge of ₹0 % is levied
explain: Under Section 65 and MOOWR Scheme 2019, if resultant products are exported, import duties on the inputs utilized in manufacturing are completely remitted, and no duty is paid on capital goods used in the warehouse. (Source: Section 65 Customs Act / MOOWR Regs 2019)
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 65 - Manufacture in Warehouse (MOOWR)

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 68 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what document must be presented for clearance of warehoused goods for home consumption?
options: Bill of Entry for Home Consumption (White Form)
Bill of Entry for Ex-Bond Clearance (Green Form) accompanied by payment of duty, interest, and warehouse charges
explain: Section 68 requires the importer to present an Ex-Bond Bill of Entry (traditionally on green paper) for home consumption and pay the assessed import duty, penalties, interest, and storage charges before clearance order is made. (Source: Section 68 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 68 - Ex-Bond Bill of Entry

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section ₹28 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , within what time period from the date of communication of an adjudication order (passed by an officer lower than Commissioner) must an appeal be filed before the Commissioner (Appeals)?
options: 60 days from the date of communication (extendable by a further period of 30 days by Commissioner (Appeals) on sufficient cause)
explain: Section ₹28 (1) provides that any person aggrieved by any decision or order may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) within sixty days. The proviso permits condonation of delay by a further period of thirty days if satisfied with sufficient cause. (Source: Section ₹28 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 128 - Appeal to Commissioner (Appeals)

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962 , what percentage of the duty or penalty in dispute must be mandatorily pre-deposited for an appeal before Commissioner (Appeals) and CESTAT respectively?
options: Commissioner (Appeals): 7.5%; CESTAT: 7.5% (for first stage) and ₹0 % (for second stage against Commissioner (Appeals) order), subject to Rs ₹0 Crore ceiling
explain: Section 129E mandates a pre-deposit of: (i) 7.5% of duty/penalty for appeal before Commissioner (Appeals), (ii) 7.5% for appeal before CESTAT against an order of Commissioner, and (iii) ₹0 % for appeal before CESTAT against an order of Commissioner (Appeals), capped at Rs ₹0 Crores. (Source: Section 129E Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129E - Mandatory Pre-Deposit

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under the proviso to Section 129A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , CESTAT may in its discretion refuse to admit an appeal where the duty or penalty involved does not exceed what threshold?
explain: The second proviso to Section 129A(1) empowers the Appellate Tribunal in its discretion to refuse to admit an appeal where the amount of duty, fine, or penalty determined by the order does not exceed two lakh rupees (₹2,00,000). (Source: Section 129A(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A - CESTAT Monetary Limit

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under the first proviso to Section 129A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , which types of orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) CANNOT be appealed before CESTAT, and are instead subject to Revision under Section 129DD?
options: Orders relating to baggage clearance, short-landing/short-shipment of goods, and payment of drawback under Chapter X
Orders relating to classification of high-tech semiconductors
Orders relating to SEZ DTA sales
explain: Under Section 129A(1) first proviso, no appeal lies to CESTAT from an order of Commissioner (Appeals) relating to: (a) goods imported/exported as baggage, (b) short-landing of goods, and (c) duty drawback. These are subject to Revision Application before the Central Government under Section 129DD. (Source: Section 129A(1) & 129DD Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A - Matched Revision Cases

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section ₹30 of the Customs Act, 1962 , on what grounds does an appeal lie from an order of CESTAT to the High Court?
options: On any minor factual disagreement regarding dock tally
Only if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law (not being an order relating to determination of rate of duty or value for purposes of assessment)
CESTAT orders are final and cannot be appealed anywhere
On grounds of delay in translation of documents
explain: Section ₹30 (1) allows an appeal to the High Court from every order of the Appellate Tribunal on a substantial question of law, provided the order does not relate to determination of the rate of duty or value of goods for assessment (which go directly to the Supreme Court under Section 130E). (Source: Section ₹30 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 130 - Appeal to High Court

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹04 of the Customs Act, 1962 , when is an offence under Section ₹35 cognizable and non-bailable?
options: Customs offences are never non-bailable under any circumstances
Only if the person refuses to sign an attendance register
All customs offences are always cognizable and non-bailable regardless of amount

Offences relating to evasion of duty exceeding ₹50 Lakhs, or prohibited goods under Section ₹1 , or fraudulent drawback exceeding ₹50 Lakhs, or specified sensitive goods (gold/firearms) are non-bailable
explain: Under Section ₹04 (6), offences punishable under Section ₹35 relating to: (a) prohibited goods, (b) evasion of duty or fraudulent drawback exceeding ₹50 Lakhs, or (c) fraudulently availing exemption exceeding ₹50 Lakhs are non-bailable and cognizable. (Source: Section ₹04 (6) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 104 - Power to Arrest & Bail

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹35 (1)(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the maximum term of imprisonment for evasion of customs duty or misdeclaration where the market price of goods or duty evaded exceeds ₹50 Lakhs?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven (7) years and with fine (minimum three years imprisonment in absence of special reasons)
explain: Section ₹35 (1)(i) provides that where the offence involves prohibited goods or duty evaded or market price exceeding fifty lakh rupees, the person shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine. (Source: Section ₹35 (1)(i) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 135 - Imprisonment Threshold

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹37 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , who is statutorily authorized to sanction criminal prosecution for offences under Sections ₹32 to 135A?
options: Any Inspector or Appraiser on port duty
The State Minister for Home Affairs
The Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs
The Chairman of Port Trust Authority
explain: Section ₹37 (1) mandates that no court shall take cognizance of any offence under Sections ₹32 , ₹33 , ₹34 , ₹35 , or 135A, except with the previous sanction of the Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs. (Source: Section ₹37 (1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 137 - Sanction for Prosecution

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹37 (3) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Customs (Compounding of Offences) Rules, 2005, what is the legal effect of compounding an offence?
options: The offender is barred from importing goods for life
The goods are destroyed by the military
On payment of the compounding amount determined by the Chief Commissioner, criminal proceedings pending in court against the offender abate and terminate completely
Compounding does not affect criminal proceedings
explain: Section ₹37 (3) read with Compounding Rules 2005 provides that upon payment of the compounding amount determined by the compounding authority, any criminal proceedings in respect of the compounded offence shall abate and no prosecution can be instituted. (Source: Section ₹37 (3) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 137(3) - Compounding of Offences

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
section: Rule 1 - Terms of Headings and Notes
text: Under Rule 1 of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , what is the legal status of titles of Sections, Chapters, and Sub-Chapters?
options: They have binding legal force and override heading text
They determine the rate of IGST exclusively
They are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes
They are meant only for port labor unions
explain: Rule 1 explicitly states that the titles of Sections, Chapters and Sub-Chapters are provided for ease of reference only; for legal purposes, classification shall be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes. (Source: GIR Rule 1 / Customs Tariff Act, 1975 )
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 1 - Terms of Headings and Notes

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 2(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation, how is an incomplete or unfinished article classified if, as presented, it has the essential character of the complete or finished article?
options: It must be classified under as Project Imports
It shall be classified under the same heading as the complete or finished article, including when presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD)
It cannot be classified until completely assembled in India
explain: Rule 2(a) provides that any reference in a heading to an article shall be taken to include a reference to that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that, as presented, the incomplete or unfinished article has the essential character of the complete or finished article, including knocked down condition. (Source: GIR Rule 2(a))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 2(a) - Incomplete and Unassembled Articles

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation, when goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, which principle governs?
options: The importer can choose any heading at will
The heading with the highest alphanumeric number must be chosen
The heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description
The heading with the lowest duty rate must be chosen
explain: Rule 3(a) provides that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description. (Source: GIR Rule 3(a) / Customs Tariff Act, 1975 )
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(a) - Specific over General Description

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation, how are mixtures, composite goods consisting of different materials, and goods put up in sets for retail sale classified?
options: As if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their 'essential character', insofar as this criterion is applicable
By taking an arithmetic average of all components
Always under the heading for packaging materials
Always under the residual heading of
explain: Rule 3(b) provides that mixtures, composite goods, and retail sets which cannot be classified by reference to 3(a) shall be classified as if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their essential character. (Source: GIR Rule 3(b))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(b) - Essential Character Principle

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3(c) of the General Rules for Interpretation, when goods cannot be classified by reference to Rule 3(a) or 3(b), how shall they be classified?
options: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
Under the heading which occurs first in numerical order
Under the heading suggested by the Chamber of Commerce
explain: Rule 3(c) explicitly dictates that when goods cannot be classified by reference to Rule 3(a) or 3(b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration. (Source: GIR Rule 3(c))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3(c) - Last in Numerical Order

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 4 of the General Rules for Interpretation, goods which cannot be classified in accordance with Rules 1, 2, or 3 shall be classified under:
options: Any heading chosen by the port custodian
The heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin
explain: Rule 4 provides that goods which cannot be classified in accordance with Rules 1, 2 or 3 shall be classified under the heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin. (Source: GIR Rule 4 / Customs Tariff Act, 1975 )
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 4 - Most Akin Principle

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 5(a) of the General Rules for Interpretation, when are camera cases, musical instrument cases, gun cases, and similar specially fitted containers classified along with the article?
options: Fitted cases must always be assessed separately under

When specially shaped or fitted to contain a specific article, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles for which they are intended (provided they do not give the whole its essential character)
Only if imported by diplomatic personnel
Only if they are manufactured from solid wood
explain: Rule 5(a) provides that cases and containers specially shaped/fitted, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles shall be classified with such articles, unless the container gives the whole its essential character. (Source: GIR Rule 5(a))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 5(a) - Fitted Cases and Containers

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 5(b) of the General Rules for Interpretation, what is the statutory exception regarding packing containers presented with goods?
options: Containers must be re-exported within 24 hours
Paper cartons are always assessed separately
All packaging must be incinerated at customs docks
Rule 5(b) is not binding when packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use (such as returnable steel gas cylinders or ISO tanks)
explain: Rule 5(b) provides that packing materials and containers presented with goods are classified with them if of a kind normally used, but this provision is not binding when such packing materials or containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use. (Source: GIR Rule 5(b))
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 5(b) - Repetitive Use Containers

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 6 of the General Rules for Interpretation, how must sub-heading classifications be compared for legal purposes?
options: Sub-heading rules override Section and Chapter Notes unconditionally
Only sub-headings at the same level are comparable (e.g. single dash with single dash, and double dash with double dash)
Sub-heading classification is determined by the municipal corporation
Any 6-digit subheading can be compared directly with any 8-digit tariff item
explain: Rule 6 specifies that the classification of goods in the sub-headings of a heading shall be determined according to the terms of those sub-headings, and only sub-headings at the same level are comparable. (Source: GIR Rule 6 / Customs Tariff Act, 1975 )
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 6 - Sub-Heading Classification

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Paragraph 1.35 of FTP 2023, what is the standard annual export turnover threshold required for a town to be notified as a Town of Export Excellence (TEE)?
options: ₹750 Crores (Rs ₹50 Crores for Handloom, Handicraft, Agriculture, and Fisheries sectors)
explain: Paragraph 1.35 provides that towns producing goods of ₹750 Crores or more may be recognized as TEE based on export potential; however, for Handloom, Handicraft, Agriculture and Fisheries sectors, the threshold is Rs ₹50 Crores. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 1.35)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 1.35 - Eligibility Benchmark

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Section 7 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, ₹992 , what is the statutory status of the Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)?
options: It is an optional marketing number issued by trade associations
No person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code number granted by the Director General or authorized officer
It is required only for exports to South America
It is granted automatically to every citizen on turning ₹8
explain: Section 7 of the FTDR Act, ₹992 mandates that no person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-exporter Code Number granted by the Director General or the officer authorised by the Director General. (Source: Section 7 FTDR Act, ₹992 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 7 - Importer-Exporter Code (IEC)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Section ₹1 (2) of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, ₹992 , what is the statutory financial penalty for contravening any provision of the Act, rules, orders, or FTP?
options: A penalty not less than ten thousand rupees and not more than five times the value of the goods or services or technology in respect of which the contravention is made
Penalty equal to ₹00 % of the company's net worth
explain: Section ₹1 (2) of the FTDR Act provides that where any person contravenes any provision of the Act, rules or orders, he shall be liable to a penalty of not less than ten thousand rupees and not more than five times the value of goods/services/technology. (Source: Section ₹1 (2) FTDR Act, ₹992 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 11(2) - Penalties for Contravention

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Section ₹5 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, ₹992 , within what time period must an appeal against an order passed by an Adjudicating Authority be preferred?
options: 45 days from the date on which the decision or order is served
