explain: Section ₹5 (1) of the FTDR Act provides that any person aggrieved by any decision or order made under the Act may prefer an appeal within forty-five days from the date on which the decision or order is served on him. (Source: Section ₹5 (1) FTDR Act, ₹992 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 15 - Appellate Authorities

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Paragraph 4.₹4 of FTP 2023, what facility can an Advance Authorisation holder avail if they decide to source duty-free inputs from indigenous domestic suppliers instead of direct importation?
options: They can obtain an Advance Release Order (ARO) or Invalidation Letter from the Regional Authority to procure inputs domestically against deemed export benefits
They can procure inputs with cash subsidies from the State Government
They must surrender their GST registration
They must cancel the Advance Authorisation and pay 50% penalty
explain: Paragraph 4.₹4 of FTP 2023 allows an Advance Authorisation holder intending to source inputs from indigenous suppliers to obtain an Advance Release Order (ARO) or Invalidation Letter, treating the supply as deemed exports. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 4.₹4 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — FTP 2023 Para 4.14 - Advance Release Order (ARO)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
section: FTP 2023 Para 7.02 - Eligible Deemed Export Categories
text: Under Paragraph 7.02 of FTP 2023, which of the following transactions qualifies as 'Deemed Exports'?
options: Supply of goods against Advance Authorisation / DFIA, supply of capital goods to EPCG authorisations, and supplies to Export Oriented Units (EOUs)
Supply of passenger vehicles to private taxi drivers
Sale of goods across retail counters in domestic shopping malls
Shipment of personal effects between two domestic cities
explain: Paragraph 7.02 defines Deemed Exports as supplies of goods manufactured in India where goods do not leave the country, including supplies against Advance Authorisation/DFIA, supplies to EOU/STP/EHTP, and supply of capital goods under EPCG. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 7.02)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 7.02 - Eligible Deemed Export Categories

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under of FTP 2023, what is the mandatory financial performance requirement that an Export Oriented Unit (EOU) must achieve over a 5-year block?
options: Zero domestic clearance throughout the entire 5 years
A positive Net Foreign Exchange Earnings (NFE) cumulatively, calculated as NFE = FOB value of exports minus CIF value of imported inputs and capital goods amortization
Minimum gross export of Rs ₹00 Crores annually
explain: Paragraph 6.04 of FTP 2023 requires that an EOU/EHTP/STP/BTP unit shall achieve positive Net Foreign Exchange Earnings (NFE) cumulatively for a period of five years from the commencement of commercial production. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 6.04)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 6.01 - Net Foreign Exchange (NFE)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Paragraph 6.08 of FTP 2023, to what extent can an EOU clear its manufactured goods into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) against concessional duties upon achieving positive NFE?
options: ₹00 % of its production can be sold in DTA unconditionally
Up to 50% of the FOB value of physical exports, on payment of applicable duties
Up to ₹0 % of FOB value of exports
DTA sales are strictly prohibited for EOUs
explain: Paragraph 6.08 of FTP 2023 permits EOUs to sell up to 50% of FOB value of physical exports into the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) on payment of applicable duties, provided the unit maintains positive NFE. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 6.08)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 6.08 - DTA Clearance Concessions

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under of FTP 2023, which specific export sectors are eligible for the RoSCTL (Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies) Scheme?
options: Only mineral ores and petroleum products
Apparel and garments (ITC HS Chapters 61 and 62) and Made-up textile articles (ITC HS )
Iron and steel bars and billets
explain: The RoSCTL scheme is specifically notified for the export of garments and apparels (Chapters 61 & 62) and made-ups () to rebate embedded central and state taxes like State VAT, mandi tax, and electricity duty. (Source: FTP 2023 / Ministry of Textiles Notif)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 4.01 - Scope of RoSCTL

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
section: FTP 2023 Para 2.52 - Rupee Invoicing and Vostro Accounts
text: Under Paragraph 2.52 of FTP 2023 and RBI Circular A.P. (DIR Series) No. ₹0 , how may international trade transactions be settled in Indian Rupees (INR)?
options: Through Special Non-Resident Rupee (SNRR) and Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVA) opened by foreign correspondent banks with Authorized Dealer (AD) banks in India
Only through barter arrangements of gold coins
Settlement in INR for foreign trade is prohibited under Indian law
By carrying physical Indian currency notes across borders
explain: Paragraph 2.52 of FTP 2023 and RBI guidelines allow invoicing, payment, and settlement of exports and imports in INR through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVA) maintained by partner trading country banks with authorized dealer banks in India. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 2.52 / RBI Circular ₹0 /2022)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 2.52 - Rupee Invoicing and Vostro Accounts

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Paragraph 9.04 of FTP 2023, what is the enhanced consignment value ceiling for exports through courier mode to qualify for e-commerce export facilitation and FTP benefits?
options: Rs ₹0 Lakhs per consignment (increased from ₹5 Lakhs)
explain: FTP 2023 increased the consignment value limit for exports through courier from ₹5 Lakhs to Rs ₹0 Lakhs per consignment to foster growth in cross-border e-commerce exports. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 9.04)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 9.04 - Consignment Value Limit

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Paragraph 2.39 of FTP 2023, what defines 'Merchanting Trade' carried out by an Indian trader?
options: Sale of second-hand machinery within Special Economic Zones
Import of goods exclusively for free distribution
Wholesale retail trade in local vegetable mandis
Shipment of goods from one foreign country to another foreign country without the goods entering Indian customs territory, involving an Indian intermediary and compliance with RBI guidelines
explain: Paragraph 2.39 permits Merchanting Trade where goods are procured from one foreign country and shipped directly to another foreign country without entering the domestic customs territory of India, subject to RBI guidelines. (Source: FTP 2023 Para 2.39)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — FTP 2023 Para 2.39 - Merchanting Trade Criteria

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: How is the Export Obligation under an EPCG authorisation structured across the 6-year validity period under the Handbook of Procedures 2023?
options: Block 1 (Years 1 to 4): Minimum 50% of total EO; Block 2 (Years 5 and 6): Remaining 50% of total EO
Equal ₹6 .66% in each of the 6 years strictly
No interim target; all ₹00 % can be completed on the final day of the 6th year
₹00 % must be fulfilled in the first year
explain: Paragraph 5.₹2 of HBP 2023 mandates block-wise EO fulfillment: in the first block (1st to 4th year), at least 50% of total EO must be fulfilled, and in the second block (5th and 6th year), the balance 50% must be fulfilled. (Source: HBP 2023 Para 5.₹2 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — FTP 2023 Para 5.04 - Block-wise EO Fulfillment

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Notification No. ₹1 /2004-Customs, what is the duty-free concession granted to passengers importing a laptop computer (notebook computer)?
options: One laptop computer (notebook computer) imported by any passenger of age ₹8 years or above (other than crew member) is completely exempt from customs duty over and above the GFA
Laptops can only be imported under an Advance Authorisation
Up to five laptops can be imported duty-free by any child
Laptops are subject to 50% customs duty
explain: Notification No. ₹1 /2004-Customs grants full exemption from basic customs duty and IGST to one laptop computer imported by any passenger of the age of ₹8 years or above (other than member of crew) in their baggage. (Source: Notif ₹1 /2004-Cus / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Notification No. 11/2004-Customs - Laptop Exemption

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Section 80 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what facility is provided to an incoming passenger carrying dutiable or prohibited baggage that they do not intend into India?
options: The baggage must be confiscated and destroyed immediately
The passenger must pay double duty and forfeit the goods
The baggage is auctioned within 24 hours
At the request of the passenger, the baggage may be detained by customs for the purpose of being returned to him when he leaves India
explain: Section 80 provides that where the baggage of a passenger contains any article which is dutiable or prohibited, the proper officer may, at the request of the passenger, detain such article for the purpose of being returned to him on his leaving India. (Source: Section 80 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 80 - Temporary Detention of Baggage

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 74(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what percentage of import duty is refunded as drawback when imported goods are re-exported without being used in India?
explain: Section 74(1) provides that when goods capable of being easily identified which have been imported into India and upon which duties have been paid are exported without having been used in India, ninety-eight percent (98%) of such duty shall be repaid as drawback. (Source: Section 74(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(1) - Unused Goods Re-Export Drawback

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 74(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Notification No. ₹9 /65-Customs, what is the maximum period of use in India beyond which NO drawback is payable upon re-exportation?
explain: Under Notification No. ₹9 /65-Customs as amended, where goods are used in India prior to re-export, the drawback percentage reduces in 3-month slabs down to 60% for ₹5 -₹8 months; if the period of use exceeds ₹8 months, drawback is NIL. (Source: Notif ₹9 /65-Cus / Section 74(2))
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(2) - Drawback on Used Goods

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 75A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , if duty drawback is not paid to the claimant within what statutory period from the date of filing the claim, must interest @ 6% per annum be paid to the claimant?
options: One (1) month from the date of filing the claim
explain: Section 75A(1) provides that where any drawback payable to a claimant under Section 74 or 75 is not paid within a period of one month from the date of filing the claim, interest @ 6% per annum shall be payable to the claimant from the expiry of the said period of one month till payment. (Source: Section 75A(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 75A - Interest on Delayed Drawback

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 76 of the Customs Act, 1962 , under which of the following statutory conditions is the grant of duty drawback completely prohibited?
options: If the drawback claim is submitted electronically
If the goods are shipped on an Indian flag vessel
If the goods are exported to a European nation
In respect of any goods the market-price of which is less than the amount of drawback claimed, or where the drawback claim in respect of any shipment is less than fifty rupees (₹50)
explain: Section 76(1) bars drawback: (a) where market price is less than drawback amount, (b) where the drawback due on any single shipment is less than ₹50, or (c) where goods are likely to be smuggled back into India. (Source: Section 76 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 76 - Prohibitions on Drawback Grant

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Notification No. ₹58 /95-Customs, when Indian manufactured goods are exported and subsequently re-imported for repairs, what is the maximum permissible time frame within which the repaired goods must be re-exported back?
options: 6 months (extendable up to one year by the Commissioner of Customs)
explain: Notification No. ₹58 /95-Customs allows duty-free re-import of Indian goods for repairs or reconditioning on execution of a bond, subject to the condition that the goods are re-exported within 6 months (extendable up to one year by Commissioner). (Source: Notif ₹58 /95-Cus / Section 20)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 20 / Notification No. 158/95-Customs

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Notification No. 45/2017-Customs, when goods exported under duty drawback or refund of IGST are re-imported into India without any alteration, what customs duty is payable upon re-importation?
options: Full Basic Customs Duty and IGST as if the goods were originally manufactured abroad
The amount of duty drawback or IGST refund availed at the time of export must be repaid, along with applicable interest
Completely nil duty without any repayment
explain: Notification No. 45/2017-Customs prescribes that when goods exported under drawback, IGST refund, or duty exemption schemes are re-imported, the importer must repay the export incentive/drawback/refund availed at the time of export. (Source: Notif 45/2017-Cus / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Notification No. 45/2017-Customs

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, what is the standard time limit within which full value of export goods must be realized and repatriated to India?
options: Nine (9) months from the date of export (₹5 months in case of goods exported to a warehouse established outside India)
3 months from the date of export
explain: Regulation 9 of FEMA Export Regulations 2015 provides that the amount representing the full export value of goods shall be realized and repatriated to India within nine months from the date of export (or ₹5 months if exported to an overseas storage warehouse). (Source: RBI Master Direction - Export of Goods and Services)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Regulation 9 - Export Realization Time Period

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: What is the function of the EDPMS (Export Data Processing and Monitoring System) and IDPMS (Import Data Processing and Monitoring System) operated by the Reserve Bank of India in coordination with Customs?
options: To electronically reconcile customs shipping bills and bills of entry with inward and outward foreign exchange banking remittances, tracking unmatched payments and cautions
To track physical shipping container GPS coordinates in ocean waters
To calculate personal income tax liabilities of port pilots
To process tourist visa applications at airports
explain: EDPMS and IDPMS are RBI IT platforms integrated with ICEGATE to track and reconcile customs declarations (Shipping Bills and Bills of Entry) with actual cross-border inward and outward foreign exchange remittances processed by AD banks. (Source: RBI / CBIC Circulars)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — EDPMS and IDPMS Monitoring Systems

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017, what is the mandatory minimum remaining shelf-life required for imported food consignments at the time of customs import clearance?
options: There is no shelf-life restriction for imported packaged foods
Not less than 60% of its original shelf-life (or three months, whichever is less) at the time of import clearance
explain: Regulation 5(6) of FSSAI (Import) Regulations 2017 mandates that customs shall not clear any food consignment unless it has a valid remaining shelf-life of not less than 60% (or three months, whichever is less) at the time of clearance. (Source: FSSAI Import Regulations, 2017)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5 - Minimum Remaining Shelf Life

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the FSSAI (Import) Regulations, 2017, which of the following labeling deficiencies can be rectified by an importer inside a customs bonded warehouse prior to visual inspection and sampling?
options: Altering the list of ingredients and country of origin
Affixing a single non-detachable sticker stating: Name and address of importer, FSSAI Logo and License Number, and Non-Veg/Veg Logo
Change of expiry date and nutritional value tables
No labeling rectification is ever permitted in customs areas
explain: Under FSSAI guidelines and Regulation 6, rectifiable defects permitted to be corrected in customs bonded warehouses via a sticker are: (a) Importer name and address, (b) FSSAI logo and license number, and (c) Veg/Non-Veg logo. Core facts like expiry date and ingredients cannot be altered. (Source: FSSAI Order No. 1-₹782 /FSSAI/Imports/2018)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Regulation 6 - Rectifiable Labeling Defects

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, which mandatory declarations must be displayed on every pre-packaged commodity imported into India?
options: The political affiliation of the overseas exporter
Only the name of the foreign shipping vessel

Name and address of manufacturer and importer, generic name of commodity, net quantity in standard metric units, month and year of manufacture/import, Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and consumer care contacts
The wholesale dealer price excluding GST
explain: Rule 6 of Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules 2011 mandates that all imported pre-packaged packages must display: importer name/address, generic name, net quantity, date of import/manufacture, Maximum Retail Price (MRP inclusive of all taxes), and customer helpline. (Source: Legal Metrology Rules, 2011 / CBIC Circular 33/2017-Cus)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under the Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003, what official documentation is mandatory for import clearance of agricultural consignments and timber?
options: A Certificate of Fitness from the local municipal corporation
A tourist brochure from the country of origin
An official Phytosanitary Certificate (PSC) issued by the National Plant Protection Organization (NPPO) of the exporting country certifying freedom from quarantine pests and weed seeds
explain: Under the PQ Order 2003, all agricultural seeds, plants, produce, and unprocessed wood/timber must be accompanied by an official Phytosanitary Certificate issued by the exporting country's NPPO and meet import permit phytosanitary conditions. (Source: PQ Order, 2003 / Directorate of Plant Protection)
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — PQ Order, 2003 - Phytosanitary Certificate

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
section: Rule 43A - Designated Ports of Import for Drugs
text: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, ₹945 , how is the import of bulk drugs and pharmaceutical formulations into India restricted geographically?
options: Drugs can only enter through parcel post from neighboring countries
Import of drugs is restricted strictly to designated notified customs ports, airports, and ICDs equipped with CDSCO Port Drug Control offices (e.g. Mumbai, Nhava Sheva, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi)
Drugs can be imported through any minor private jetty across India
Drugs can be unloaded at any dry dock without customs intervention
explain: Rule 43A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, ₹945 restricts the importation of drugs into India exclusively to notified ports and airports where CDSCO Assistant Drug Controllers are posted for inspection, verification of Form ₹0 import license, and NOC issuance. (Source: Rule 43A Drugs & Cosmetics Rules, ₹945 )
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 43A - Designated Ports of Import for Drugs

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance (GFA) for an Indian resident or a foreigner residing in India arriving by air from countries other than Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar?
explain: Rule 3 of Baggage Rules 2016 provides that an Indian resident or foreigner residing in India arriving by air or sea from countries other than Nepal, Bhutan or Myanmar is entitled to a General Free Allowance (GFA) of ₹50,000 for dutiable articles. (Source: Rule 3 Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 - General Free Allowance (GFA)

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
section: Rule 4 - Tourist of Foreign Origin GFA
text: Under Rule 4 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what is the General Free Allowance permitted to a tourist of foreign origin arriving in India?
explain: Rule 4 of Baggage Rules 2016 provides that a tourist of foreign origin (other than from Nepal, Bhutan, or Myanmar) is entitled used personal effects and travel souvenirs, plus other articles up to a value of Rs ₹5,000 duty-free. (Source: Rule 4 Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 4 - Tourist of Foreign Origin GFA

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Rule 5 of the Baggage Rules, 2016, what are the permissible duty-free jewellery allowances for a gentleman and a lady passenger respectively who have resided abroad for over one year?
options: Both are allowed up to ₹00 grams without any value ceiling
Gentleman: up to 20 grams with a value cap of ₹50,000; Lady: up to 40 grams with a value cap of ₹1,00,000
explain: Rule 5 provides that a passenger residing abroad for more than one year may bring duty-free jewellery: gentleman passenger up to 20 grams (value ceiling ₹50,000); lady passenger up to 40 grams (value ceiling ₹1,00,000). (Source: Rule 5 Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Rule 5 - Jewellery Allowance Limits

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Which of the following items is listed under Annexure I of Baggage Rules, 2016 and therefore CANNOT be imported under the General Free Allowance (GFA)?
options: Firearms, cartridges exceeding 50, cigarettes exceeding ₹00 sticks, alcoholic liquor exceeding 2 litres, gold or silver in any form other than ornaments
explain: Annexure I items cannot be cleared under GFA: firearms, cartridges in excess of 50, cigarettes in excess of ₹00 or cigars in excess of 25 or tobacco in excess of 125g, alcoholic liquor/wines in excess of 2 litres, gold/silver in bars/bullion, and flat panel TVs. (Source: Annexure I Baggage Rules, 2016)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Annexure I - Non-GFA Dutiable Goods

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
section: Section 46(3) - Bill of Entry Filing Timeline
text: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 , by when must the importer present the Bill of Entry on the Common Portal?
options: Only after the cargo has been unstuffed into a CFS
Before the end of the day (including holidays) preceding the day on which the aircraft or vessel or vehicle carrying the goods arrives at a customs station
Any time within one year from unloading
Within 30 days after arrival of the ship
explain: Section 46(3) mandates that the importer shall present the bill of entry before the end of the day (including holidays) preceding the day on which the aircraft, vessel, or vehicle arrives at the customs station where goods are to be cleared. (Source: Section 46(3) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3) - Bill of Entry Filing Timeline

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under Regulation 4 of the Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration and Paperless Processing) Regulations, 2018, what late fees are payable for delay in presenting the Bill of Entry?
options: ₹5,000 per day for the initial three days of default, and Rs ₹0,000 per day for each subsequent day of default
explain: Under the Bill of Entry Regulations 2018, late filing charges are prescribed as ₹5,000 per day for the first three days of delay, and Rs ₹0,000 per day for each day thereafter until presentation of the bill of entry. (Source: Bill of Entry Regulations, 2018 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Late Filing Charges

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under Section 47(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , within what time limit must the importer pay the assessed customs duty to avoid liability for interest under Section 28AA?
options: Within 30 days of arrival of cargo
On the date of presentation of the bill of entry in the case of self-assessment, or within one day (excluding holidays) from the date on which the bill of entry is returned for payment of duty
Within ₹5 working days from grant of Out of Charge
explain: Section 47(2) provides that the importer shall pay the duty: (a) on the date of presentation in self-assessment, or (b) within one day (excluding holidays) from the date of return of bill of entry by the proper officer for payment; failing which interest @ ₹5 % p.a. is payable. (Source: Section 47(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 47(2) - Duty Payment Deadline

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under Section ₹7 (5) of the Customs Act, 1962 , where the proper officer re-assesses duty contrary to the self-assessment and the importer does not confirm acceptance in writing, within what period must the officer issue a speaking order?
options: Within fifteen (₹5 ) days from the date of re-assessment of the bill of entry or the shipping bill
explain: Section ₹7 (5) provides that where any re-assessment done under subsection (4) is contrary to the self-assessment and the importer/exporter has not confirmed acceptance in writing, the proper officer shall pass a speaking order within ₹5 days. (Source: Section ₹7 (5) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 17(5) - Speaking Order on Re-Assessment

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under Section 51 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what statutory order must the proper officer make before export goods can be permitted to be loaded on a conveyance for exportation?
options: Let Export Order (LEO) permitting clearance and loading of the goods
No Objection Certificate from Port Trust
explain: Section 51 provides that where the proper officer is satisfied that goods are not prohibited and export duties/charges are paid, he shall make an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation, known as 'Let Export Order' (LEO). (Source: Section 51 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 51 - Let Export Order (LEO)

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: What is the primary role of a Turant Suvidha Kendra (TSK) established at Customs Stations under the Turant Customs / Faceless Assessment initiative?
options: To conduct criminal interrogations of passengers
To act as a single-point facilitation center for trade to submit physical documents, bonds, bank guarantees, debit bonds, and obtain physical prints without visiting multiple assessment groups
To inspect physical cargo in shipping containers
explain: Turant Suvidha Kendras (TSK) were set up under Circular No. 28/2020-Customs as dedicated touchpoints at all customs ports to facilitate physical bond execution, bank guarantee debit/credit, and trade queries in a faceless environment. (Source: CBIC Circular 28/2020-Cus)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Turant Suvidha Kendra (TSK)

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under the e-SANCHIT (e-Storage and Computerized Handling of Indirect Tax documents) facility on ICEGATE, what is an 'IRN'?
options: Image Reference Number, generated as a unique digital identifier upon uploading a supporting document in PDF format on e-SANCHIT, which is then tagged to the Bill of Entry
explain: On e-SANCHIT, when an importer or Customs Broker digitally signs and uploads a supporting document in PDF, the ICEGATE portal generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN), which is then linked in the Bill of Entry declaration. (Source: CBIC Circular 40/2017-Cus)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Image Reference Number (IRN)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Section 3(7) and 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , how is the value for the levy of Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) computed on imported goods?
options: Retail Sale Price declared on the package
Assessable Value under Section ₹4 PLUS Basic Customs Duty (BCD) PLUS any other applicable cesses (excluding IGST and GST Compensation Cess itself)
explain: Section 3(8) provides that the value of imported goods for levying IGST under subsection (7) shall be the aggregate of the assessable value determined under Section ₹4 and any duty of customs chargeable thereon (including BCD and SWS, but excluding IGST and Compensation Cess). (Source: Section 3(8) CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 3(7) - IGST Computation Base

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Section 8B of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , on what statutory ground does the Central Government impose Safeguard Duty on an imported article?
options: When any article is being imported into India in such increased quantities (absolute or relative to domestic production) and under such conditions as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to domestic industry
When the foreign exporter is selling goods below fair market value
When the country of export devalues its national currency
When the importer has failed to pay GST
explain: Section 8B(1) authorizes the Central Government to impose safeguard duty if satisfied that an article is being imported in increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic industry producing like or directly competitive articles. (Source: Section 8B CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 8B - Safeguard Duty

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
section: Section 9 - Countervailing Duty on Subsidized Goods
text: Under Section 9 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , what is the maximum duration of a Countervailing Duty (CVD) imposed on subsidized articles imported into India?
options: Five (5) years from the date of its imposition (subject to extension for a further 5 years upon a sunset review)
explain: Section 9(4) provides that countervailing duty on subsidized goods shall cease to have effect on the expiry of five years from the date of its imposition, unless extended for another period of five years following a review (sunset review). (Source: Section 9(4) CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9 - Countervailing Duty on Subsidized Goods

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Section 9A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , what is the statutory ceiling on the Anti-Dumping Duty that can be levied on dumped imported goods?
options: The duty shall not exceed the margin of dumping in relation to such article (Margin of Dumping = Normal Value in exporting country minus Export Price to India)
The duty cannot exceed the total ocean freight
The duty cannot exceed 25% of CIF value
The duty is fixed uniformly at USD ₹00 per metric ton
explain: Section 9A(1) prescribes that the anti-dumping duty imposed shall not exceed the margin of dumping determined in relation to the article, where margin of dumping is the difference between normal value and export price. (Source: Section 9A CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9A - Anti-Dumping Duty (ADD)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
section: Section 9C - Appeal to CESTAT against ADD/CVD
text: Under Section 9C of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , within what time limit must an appeal against an order of determination or review of Anti-Dumping Duty or Countervailing Duty be filed before CESTAT?
options: Ninety (90) days from the date of the order under appeal
explain: Section 9C(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 provides that an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against an order of determination regarding existence, degree, and effect of dumping or subsidy shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order. (Source: Section 9C CTA 1975 )
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9C - Appeal to CESTAT against ADD/CVD

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Section ₹10 of the Finance Act, 2018, how is the Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) calculated on imported goods?
options: ₹0 % of the total CIF value of the shipment
Ten percent (₹0 %) calculated on the aggregate of duties, taxes, and cesses levied under Section ₹2 of the Customs Act (specifically Basic Customs Duty), excluding IGST and Compensation Cess
explain: Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) is levied @ ₹0 % on the aggregate of customs duties (primarily Basic Customs Duty). It is NOT levied on Integrated Tax (IGST) or GST Compensation Cess. (Source: Section ₹10 Finance Act, 2018 / CBIC Circular)
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section ₹3 of the Customs Act, 1962 , when is an importer NOT liable to pay customs duty on pilfered goods?
options: If the goods were insured under a marine policy
Only if the thief is convicted by a criminal court
If goods are pilfered at any time within 5 years after clearance

If any imported goods are pilfered after the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, and the goods are not restored to the importer
explain: Section ₹3 provides that if imported goods are pilfered after unloading and before an order for clearance for home consumption or warehousing is made, the importer shall not be liable to pay the duty thereon unless the goods are restored. (Source: Section ₹3 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 13 - Pilfered Goods

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 22 of the Customs Act, 1962 , how is the customs duty determined on imported goods that have sustained damage or deterioration before or during unloading?
options: Goods are exempt from all duty unconditionally
Duty is replaced by a flat port storage fee
Full duty must be paid without any deduction
Duty is charged proportionately to the diminished value, calculated as duty on undamaged value multiplied by the ratio of damaged value to undamaged value
explain: Section 22(1) allows abatement of duty on goods damaged/deteriorated before or during unloading, or in warehouse before clearance; duty chargeable is reduced in proportion to the diminution in value determined by the proper officer. (Source: Section 22 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 22 - Abatement on Damaged Goods

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 23(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory provision regarding duty on goods lost or destroyed before clearance?
options: The importer must pay double duty as penalty

Where it is shown to the satisfaction of the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs that any imported goods have been lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption, the officer shall remit the duty
Duty is refunded only after an inquiry by the Supreme Court
The shipping line is arrested automatically
explain: Section 23(1) mandates remission of duty where goods are lost (otherwise than by pilferage) or destroyed by accidental fire, flood, or natural cause at any time before clearance for home consumption. (Source: Section 23(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 23(1) - Goods Lost or Destroyed

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , up to what point can the owner of imported goods relinquish title to the goods to avoid paying customs duty?
options: Relinquishment of title is barred under Indian law
Only before the ship arrives in Indian territorial waters
At any time within three years after clearing the goods home

At any time before an order for clearance of goods for home consumption under Section 47 or an order for permitting deposit of goods in a warehouse under Section 60 has been made, provided no offence has been committed
explain: Section 23(2) allows the owner to relinquish his title to the goods at any time before an order for clearance under Section 47 or deposit in a warehouse under Section 60 is made, and thereupon he shall not be liable to pay duty (proviso bars relinquishment if offence is committed). (Source: Section 23(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 23(2) - Relinquishment of Title

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 27(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory time limit for an importer or exporter to make an application for refund of duty and interest to the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs?
options: One (1) year from the date of payment of duty and interest (or date of final assessment in case of provisional assessment)
explain: Section 27(1) provides that any person claiming refund of duty or interest shall make an application within one year from the date of payment of such duty or interest, or from the date of adjustment of duty after final assessment under Section ₹8 . (Source: Section 27(1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 27 - Limitation Period for Refund

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
section: Section 27(2) - Consumer Welfare Fund & Unjust Enrichment
text: Under Section 27(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 (Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment), where is a sanctioned customs refund credited if the claimant fails to establish that they did not pass on the duty incidence to their buyers?
options: To the Port Trust Pension Fund
To the Reserve Bank of India general reserve
To the Consumer Welfare Fund established under Section 57 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
It is forfeited and converted into foreign exchange
explain: Under Section 27(2), if the applicant is unable to establish that the incidence of duty/interest has not been passed on to any other person, the refundable amount is credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund instead of being paid to the applicant. (Source: Section 27(2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 27(2) - Consumer Welfare Fund & Unjust Enrichment

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 27A of the Customs Act, 1962 , if duty ordered to be refunded is not refunded within what period from the date of receipt of the application, must interest @ 6% per annum be paid to the applicant?
options: Three (3) months from the date of receipt of the refund application
explain: Section 27A provides that if any duty ordered to be refunded under Section 27(2) is not refunded within three months from the date of receipt of application, interest @ 6% per annum shall be payable to the applicant from the expiry of three months till refund. (Source: Section 27A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 27A - Interest on Delayed Refunds

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962 , if imported goods are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within what statutory period from unloading, may the custodian sell the goods after notice to the importer and with customs permission?
options: Thirty (30) days from the date of unloading (or such further time as the proper officer may allow, or shorter period for arms/perishables)
explain: Section 48 provides that if any goods brought into India are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within thirty days from the date of unloading, the custodian may, after notice to importer and permission from proper officer, sell the goods. (Source: Section 48 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 48 - Unclaimed Cargo Disposal

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section ₹50 (2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , in what statutory order of priority must the proceeds of sale of unclaimed or confiscated goods be applied?
options: First to customs duty, then to importer profit
First to expenses of sale, second to freight and charges payable to the carrier, third to charges payable to the custodian/warehouse keeper, and fourth to customs duty payable on the goods
Entire proceeds are paid directly to the foreign exporter
First to the municipal tax, second to the police department
explain: Section ₹50 (2) specifies the statutory hierarchy: (a) sale expenses, (b) carrier freight/charges, (c) custodian/storage charges, (d) customs duty and charges, (e) any other amount due to Central Government; balance paid to owner. (Source: Section ₹50 (2) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 150 - Application of Sale Proceeds

chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
text: Under Section 30(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with SCMTR 2018, by when must the person-in-charge of a vessel deliver the Import Manifest / Arrival Manifest to the proper officer?
options: Any time before departure of the vessel
Only when cargo unloading is completed
Prior to the arrival of the vessel at the customs port (before departure from the last port of call in case of short sea voyages)
explain: Section 30(1) requires the person-in-charge of a vessel or aircraft to deliver an import manifest electronically prior to arrival of the conveyance at the customs station, ensuring pre-arrival risk analysis and advance filing. (Source: Section 30 Customs Act, 1962 / SCMTR 2018)
topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Section 30 - Delivery of Import Manifest

chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
text: Under Section 31(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what statutory permission must be granted by the proper officer before the master of a vessel can permit the unloading of any imported goods?
options: Entry Inwards granted to the vessel
explain: Section 31(1) provides that the master of a vessel shall not permit the unloading of any imported goods until an order has been given by the proper officer granting 'Entry Inwards' to such vessel. (Source: Section 31 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Section 31 - Entry Inwards

chapter: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests
text: Under Section 42(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , under what condition may the person-in-charge of a conveyance depart from any customs station?
options: Only after the proper officer has granted a written order for Port Clearance
Upon sounding the vessel horn three times
Without any customs formalities if carrying empty containers
Whenever the pilot feels the tide is favourable
explain: Section 42(1) mandates that the person-in-charge of a conveyance which has brought any imported goods or has loaded any export goods shall not depart from that customs station without a written order of port clearance from the proper officer. (Source: Section 42 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 4: Arrival, Departure and Clearance of Conveyances; Manifests — Section 42 - Port Clearance

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 5 of CBLR, 2018, which of the following is a mandatory qualification and net worth requirement for an individual applicant?
options: Graduate from a recognized university AND a professional degree (CA/MBA/LLB/CS/CWWA) or Group A customs service experience of 2+ years, with a certified net worth of not less than five lakh rupees (₹5,00,000)
Any high school pass with net worth of ₹50,000
Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in economics with net worth of ₹1 Crore
No degree required if recommended by an existing broker
explain: Regulation 5 requires the applicant to be a citizen of India, graduate, possess professional qualification (CA/MBA/LLB/CS/ICWA etc.), and furnish a CA certificate of financial viability showing net worth of at least ₹5 Lakhs. (Source: Regulation 5 CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 5 - Educational & Financial Criteria

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 6 of CBLR, 2018, what are the passing marks for the written and oral examination respectively, and what is the maximum number of attempts allowed the examination?
options: Written: 60%; Oral: 50%; maximum six (6) attempts within a period of seven (7) years from the date of original application
explain: Regulation 6 provides that an applicant must secure at least 60% in the computer-based written exam and 50% in the oral exam, and shall be allowed a maximum of six attempts within seven years from the date of application. (Source: Regulation 6 CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 6 - Exam Structure and Attempts

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 8 of CBLR, 2018, before grant of a license in Form B, what financial bond and security must the applicant execute?
options: A cash deposit of ₹50,00,000 with the Ministry of Finance
A bond in Form D for ₹5,00,000 and a bank guarantee or postal security for five lakh rupees (₹5,00,000)
Personal undertaking on plain paper of Rs ₹0,000
explain: Regulation 8 mandates that before grant of license in Form B, the applicant shall execute a bond in Form D for ₹5,00,000 and furnish a bank guarantee or postal security for ₹5,00,000. (Source: Regulation 8 CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 8 - Security Deposit

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (a) and ₹0 (b) of CBLR, 2018, what is the statutory duty of a Customs Broker regarding client authorization?
options: The broker must obtain an authorization from each of the companies, firms or individuals by whom he is for the time being employed as Customs Broker and produce such authorization whenever required
Authorizations can be obtained orally via phone call
The broker can file declarations on behalf of any company without written authority
Authorizations must be renewed every Monday
explain: Regulation ₹0 (a) mandates that a Customs Broker shall obtain an authorization from each client by whom he is employed and produce such authorization to the proper officer whenever required. (Source: Regulation ₹0 (a) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(a) & 10(b) - Authorization & Representation

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
section: Regulation 10(d) - Advising Client and Non-Compliance Reporting
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (d) of CBLR, 2018, what must a Customs Broker do if they find that their client has not complied with the provisions of the Customs Act or rules?
options: Advise the client to comply with the provisions of the Act and rules, and in case of non-compliance, bring the matter to the notice of the Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner of Customs
Charge double brokerage fee from the client
Help the client hide the documents from the department
explain: Regulation ₹0 (d) requires the Customs Broker to advise the client to comply with the Act and rules, and if the client fails to do so, bring such non-compliance to the notice of the Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs. (Source: Regulation ₹0 (d) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(d) - Advising Client and Non-Compliance Reporting

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (n) of CBLR, 2018 (KYC Norms), what is the specific statutory obligation of a Customs Broker regarding client identity and functioning?
options: Take personal custody of the client's passport
Verify that the client belongs to the same state as the broker
Visit the client's home every weekend

Verify correctness of Importer Exporter Code (IEC) number, GSTIN, identity of his client, and functioning of his client at the declared address by using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information
explain: Regulation ₹0 (n) mandates that the Customs Broker shall verify the correctness of IEC, GSTIN, identity of the client, and functioning of the client at the declared address using reliable, independent, authentic documents/data. (Source: Regulation ₹0 (n) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(n) - KYC Due Diligence

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (l) of CBLR, 2018, what is the statutory duty of a Customs Broker regarding money received from a client for duty payment?
options: The broker can deduct a ₹0 % commission from the duty amount

The broker must ensure that all sums received from the client for payment of any duty, tax or other debt to the Government shall be promptly paid to the Government, and sums received from the Government for the client are promptly paid over
The broker may deposit the money in a fixed deposit to earn interest for 30 days
The broker can use the funds to settle another client's penalty
explain: Regulation ₹0 (l) strictly mandates that the Customs Broker shall ensure that all sums received from the client for payment of any duty, taxes or debt to the Government are promptly paid over to the Government without delay or diversion. (Source: Regulation ₹0 (l) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(l) - Prompt Payment of Duties

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹6 (1) of CBLR, 2018, when may the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs suspend the license of a Customs Broker immediately?
options: Whenever the broker changes their office furniture
Where immediate action is necessary and an inquiry against such agent is pending or contemplated, by an order in writing stating the reasons
Only after an inquiry is completed and approved by CESTAT
Whenever the broker asks for leave
explain: Regulation ₹6 (1) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in Regulation 17 , the Commissioner may, in appropriate cases where immediate action is necessary, suspend the license of a Customs Broker where an inquiry is pending or contemplated. (Source: Regulation ₹6 (1) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 16 - Immediate Suspension of License

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
section: Regulation 17 - Timeline for Notice and Inquiry
text: Under Regulation 17 of CBLR, 2018, what is the statutory time limit for the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner to issue a notice to the Customs Broker after receiving the offence report?
options: Within ninety (90) days from the date of receipt of the offence report
explain: Regulation 17 (1) mandates that the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner shall issue a notice in writing to the Customs Broker stating the grounds of allegation within ninety days from the date of receipt of the offence report. (Source: Regulation 17 (1) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 17 - Timeline for Notice and Inquiry

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 17 (5) of CBLR, 2018, within what period after receipt of the Inquiry Report must the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs pass the final order revoking the license or imposing penalty?
options: Within ninety (90) days from the date of submission of the report by the Inquiry Officer
explain: Regulation 17 (5) prescribes that the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs shall, after considering the inquiry report and representation, pass an order within ninety days from the date of submission of the inquiry report. (Source: Regulation 17 (5) CBLR, 2018)
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 17(5) - Order of Adjudication Timeline

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
section: Section 108 - Legal Nature of Summons Proceedings
text: Under Section ₹08 (4) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the legal character of an inquiry proceeding before a Gazetted Officer of Customs where a person is summoned to give evidence or produce documents?
options: It is a confidential commercial mediation
It is deemed to be a 'judicial proceeding' within the meaning of Section ₹93 and Section 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
It is equivalent to an arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act
It is an informal administrative inquiry with no legal consequences
explain: Section ₹08 (4) explicitly provides that every inquiry under Section ₹08 shall be deemed to be a 'judicial proceeding' within the meaning of Sections ₹93 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code, making intentional false statements punishable as perjury. (Source: Section ₹08 (4) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108 - Legal Nature of Summons Proceedings

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: How do statements recorded under Section ₹08 of the Customs Act, 1962 differ from statements recorded by police officers under Section ₹61 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)?
options: A statement recorded under Section ₹08 before a Gazetted Officer of Customs is substantive admissible evidence in judicial proceedings, as customs officers are not police officers under Section 25 of the Evidence Act
Statements under Section ₹08 are completely inadmissible in court
Section ₹08 statements can only be used if signed by three independent witnesses
explain: The Supreme Court has consistently held that customs officers are not 'police officers' within the meaning of Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act; therefore, voluntary statements recorded under Section ₹08 are admissible evidence in trial. (Source: Ramesh Chandra Mehta v. State of WB / Section ₹08 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108 - Admissibility of Confessional Statements

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
section: Section 103 - Power to Screen Body of Suspected Person
text: Under Section ₹03 of the Customs Act, 1962 , what statutory procedure must be followed if an officer has reason to believe that a person has smuggled goods (such as gold or narcotics) secreted inside their body?
options: Body screening is prohibited under customs law
The officer can immediately perform surgery on the spot
The person must be kept in lockup for ₹4 days without medical advice
The person must be produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay, and only with the Magistrate's order may the person's body be screened or X-rayed by a qualified medical practitioner
explain: Section ₹03 mandates that if an officer believes a person has secreted goods inside their body, the person must be produced before a Magistrate, who alone has the power to direct that the person be screened or X-rayed by a registered medical practitioner. (Source: Section ₹03 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 103 - Power to Screen Body of Suspected Person

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: What is the statutory purpose of 'Controlled Delivery' under Section 109A of the Customs Act, 1962 ?
options: Delivering cargo only using electric transport vehicles
Ensuring that government cargo is delivered without payment of ocean freight

Authorizing an officer to allow an illicit or suspect consignment of goods to pass into, through or out of India under customs supervision with a view to identifying persons involved in smuggling or illicit trafficking
Delivering cargo within 24 hours to reduce port dwell time
explain: Section 109A permits the proper officer to undertake controlled delivery of illicit or suspect consignments to identify organizers, financiers, and networks involved in smuggling, particularly narcotics and contraband. (Source: Section 109A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 109A - Controlled Delivery

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 3 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007, what is the primary basis for determining the assessable value of export goods?
options: The domestic wholesale retail price in Mumbai
The cost of raw materials plus a fixed ₹00 % markup
The international price published by the World Trade Organization

The transaction value, which is the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export from India for delivery at the time and place of exportation, where buyer and seller are not related and price is the sole consideration
explain: Rule 3(1) of Export Valuation Rules 2007 provides that the value of export goods shall be the transaction value, being the price actually paid or payable when sold for export for delivery at the time and place of exportation, provided buyer and seller are not related. (Source: Rule 3 Export Valuation Rules, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3 - Export Transaction Value

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule 4 of the Export Valuation Rules, 2007, where export value cannot be determined under Rule 3, how is value determined?
options: By assessing the goods at zero value
By requiring the exporter to auction the goods abroad
By reference to the value of goods of like kind and quality exported at or about the same time to other buyers in the same destination country (or another country with appropriate adjustments)
By taking the average price of all commodities in
explain: Rule 4 provides that the value shall be determined by comparison with the transaction value of goods of like kind and quality exported at or about the same time to other buyers in the same destination country. (Source: Rule 4 Export Valuation Rules, 2007)
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 4 - Comparison Method for Exports

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
section: Section 51A - Operation of Electronic Cash Ledger
text: Under Section 51A of the Customs Act, 1962 , how does the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) operate on the Common Portal (ICEGATE)?
options: It is a crypto-currency wallet for paying customs fines

Every deposit made by a person using authorized online payment modes or NEFT/RTGS is credited to their electronic cash ledger, and amounts from this ledger are debited to pay customs duty, interest, penalty, or fees
It can only be used by public sector oil refineries
Funds in the ECL expire if not utilized within 48 hours
explain: Section 51A establishes the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL) on ICEGATE, allowing importers, exporters, and customs brokers to maintain dynamic advance balances for instant duty and fee payment without manual challan generation. (Source: Section 51A Customs Act / ECL Regulations, 2022)
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 51A - Operation of Electronic Cash Ledger

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under Section 51B of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory status of the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger (EDCL)?
options: It is an income tax TDS certificate
It is a port labor welfare register
It is used exclusively to record physical gold imports

A ledger maintained on the customs portal where duty credits issued in lieu of remission (such as RoDTEP / RoSCTL) are credited and can be used for payment of customs duties or transferred electronically to other persons
explain: Section 51B provides for an electronic duty credit ledger on the common portal for duty credits allowed under export remission schemes, enabling electronic debit for customs duty payment or electronic transfer between IEC holders. (Source: Section 51B Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 51B - Duty Remission Scrips

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Regulation 6(1)(l) of HCCAR, 2009 read with CBIC Circular No. 22/2004-Customs, what is the custodian's legal obligation when Customs issues a Detention Certificate certifying that goods were detained for departmental investigation and no violation was found?
options: The custodian is exempt from customs jurisdiction
The custodian must sell the goods to recover expenses
The custodian must double the storage demurrage charges

The Customs Cargo Services Provider / Custodian shall not charge any demurrage or rent for the period of detention where goods are detained by customs for test or inquiry and the importer is not found at fault
explain: Regulation 6(1)(l) of HCCAR 2009 mandates that CCSPs shall not charge any rent or demurrage on goods seized or detained by the proper officer for the period of such detention where no fault is established on the part of the importer. (Source: Regulation 6(1)(l) HCCAR 2009)
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Regulation 6(1)(l) of HCCAR, 2009

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under the Customs (Fees for Rendering Services by Customs Officers) Regulations, ₹998 , when are Merchant Overtime (MOT) fees leviable on trade?
options: Whenever cargo is transported by Indian Railways
When services of customs officers are requisitioned by an importer/exporter/broker beyond working hours or on Sundays and public holidays at customs areas or private bonded warehouses
For every document filed on ICEGATE during working hours
For attending oral exams under CBLR
explain: MOT fees are levied under the ₹998 Regulations when customs officers render official services (examination, stuffing, destuffing, escort) beyond scheduled working hours or on declared holidays at the request of the trade. (Source: MOT Regulations, ₹998 / CBIC)
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Merchant Overtime (MOT) Fees

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
section: Section 147 - Liability of Principal and Agent
text: Under Section ₹47 (3) of the Customs Act, 1962 , when is an agent (such as a Customs Broker) deemed to be personally liable for customs duty or penalties in respect of goods transacted on behalf of a principal?
options: The agent must surrender all personal real estate
The agent is never liable under any circumstances
The agent is liable for ₹00 times the value of the goods

When any person is expressly or impliedly authorized by the owner, importer, or exporter to be his agent in respect of such goods, any duty, penalties, or charges recoverable from the owner may be recovered from the agent if not recovered from the owner, unless the agent proves that he acted diligently without knowledge of wrongdoing
explain: Section ₹47 (3) provides that any duty, penalty, or charges leviable on the principal may be recovered from the agent as if he were the owner, subject to statutory safeguards where the agent acted without fault or knowledge of misdeclaration. (Source: Section ₹47 (3) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 147 - Liability of Principal and Agent

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Section 146A(4) of the Customs Act, 1962 , who among the following is statutorily DISQUALIFIED from appearing as an authorized representative before any customs authority or appellate tribunal?
options: An advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of India
Any person who has been dismissed from Government service, or convicted of an offence connected with customs, or adjudged insolvent
A full-time employee of the importing company
A Chartered Accountant holding a valid Certificate of Practice
explain: Section 146A(4) explicitly bars any person who has been dismissed or removed from Government service, or convicted of any offence under customs/central excise/direct tax laws, or adjudged insolvent, from acting as an authorized representative. (Source: Section 146A(4) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 146A - Disqualifications of Authorized Representatives

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 151A of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory LIMITATION placed on the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) when issuing orders, instructions, or directions to customs officers?
options: CBIC instructions can only be issued in Hindi
CBIC cannot alter the uniform of customs officers

The Board shall NOT issue orders, instructions, or directions requiring any customs officer to make a particular assessment or dispose of a particular case in a particular manner, nor interfere with the discretion of the Commissioner (Appeals)
CBIC cannot issue any instructions on holidays
explain: The provisos to Section 151A strictly prohibit the Board from issuing directions requiring any customs officer to make a specific assessment or decide a particular case in a particular manner, thereby preserving quasi-judicial independence. (Source: Section 151A Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 151A - CBIC Instructions to Officers

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
section: Section 153 - Modes of Service of Orders & Decisions
text: Under Section ₹53 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , which of the following is a recognized legal mode of serving any order, decision, summons, or notice on a person?
options: Only through physical publication in the Gazette of India
By tender/hand delivery, registered/speed post, email to the registered email address, making it available on the Common Portal (ICEGATE), or publication in a newspaper/notice board
Sending a message via social media messenger without verification
explain: Section ₹53 (1) outlines statutory service modes: (a) physical delivery, (b) registered/speed post/courier, (c) registered email, (d) making available on the Common Customs Electronic Portal, and (e) affixture on notice board/newspaper publication. (Source: Section ₹53 (1) Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 153 - Modes of Service of Orders & Decisions

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
section: Section 143 - Power to Allow Importation on Execution of Bond
text: Under Section ₹43 of the Customs Act, 1962 , when may the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner of Customs permit the clearance of goods without production of required documents or compliance with certain formalities?
options: Upon execution by the importer of a bond with such surety or security as the officer deems fit, binding the importer to produce the documents or fulfill the conditions within a specified time limit
Without any bond if the shipment value is below ₹1 Crore
Clearance without documents is strictly prohibited under all circumstances
Only upon payment of cash bribe to the dock worker
explain: Section ₹43 empowers the proper officer to permit clearance of goods pending production of required documents or fulfillment of conditions, upon execution of a bond with appropriate surety/security binding compliance within the allowed period. (Source: Section ₹43 Customs Act, 1962 )
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 143 - Power to Allow Importation on Execution of Bond

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
text: Under the three-tier AEO Programme for importers and exporters, what percentage of bank guarantee is waived for an entity holding AEO-T2 status?
options: No waiver is granted; only fast-track clearance is provided
explain: Under CBIC Circular No. 33/2016-Customs as amended, AEO-T1 holders enjoy a 50% bank guarantee waiver, while AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 entities enjoy a ₹00 % bank guarantee waiver wherever bank guarantees are statutorily required.
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — CBIC Circular No. 33/2016-Customs

chapter: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation
text: What is the statutory validity period of an AEO Certificate issued to an entity under AEO-T1 and AEO-T2 tiers?
options: 5 years for both AEO-T1 and AEO-T2
3 years for both AEO-T1 and AEO-T2
1 year for T1 and 2 years for T2
explain: Under the AEO Programme (Circular 33/2016-Cus), certificates for AEO-T1 and AEO-T2 are valid for 3 years, whereas certificates for AEO-T3 and AEO-LO (Logistics Operators/Customs Brokers) are valid for 5 years.
topic: Chapter 20: GST on Imports and Exports, AEO and Trade Facilitation — Regulation 6 / Circular 33/2016

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
section: Section 47(1) Proviso & Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016
text: Under the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016, which category of importers is eligible to avail the benefit of deferred payment of customs duty?
options: Entities certified as AEO-T2 and AEO-T3 tier status holders
Any importer who has filed more than ₹00 Bills of Entry in a financial year
explain: Under the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016 read with Section 47(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , deferred payment facility is extended strictly to approved classes of importers, namely AEO Tier-2 and Tier-3 certified entities.
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 47(1) Proviso & Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
section: Rule 5, Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016
text: Under Rule 5 of the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016, by what date must customs duty be paid for goods cleared between the 1st and 15th day of any month (except March)?
options: By the 5th day of the succeeding month
By the 20th day of the same month
By the 16th or 17th day of the same month
By the last day of the same month
explain: Under Rule 5 of Deferred Payment Rules 2016, for bills of entry returned between 1st to 15th of a month, duty must be paid by the 16th (or 17th if ECL mode). For 16th to end of month, by 1st of next month; and for 16th to 31st March, by 31st March.
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 5, Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under the proviso to Section ₹49 of the Customs Act, 1962 , an amendment to a Bill of Entry after goods have been cleared for home consumption may be allowed only if:
options: A formal recommendation is issued by the DGFT
The differential duty involved does not exceed ₹1 Lakh
The amendment is based on documentary evidence which was in existence at the time the goods were cleared
The importer pays a mandatory compounding penalty of ₹25,000
explain: The proviso to Section ₹49 explicitly mandates that no amendment of a Bill of Entry or Shipping Bill shall be allowed after clearance, unless the amendment is substantiated by documentary evidence which was already in existence at the time the goods were cleared, deposited in a warehouse, or exported.
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Section 149 Proviso

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
