text: Under Section ₹28 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the limitation period for filing an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), and what is the maximum condonable period?
options: 60 days, condonable by further 30 days on sufficient cause
90 days, with no statutory power of condonation
explain: Section ₹28 (1) mandates that an appeal to Commissioner (Appeals) must be filed within 60 days from the date of communication of the decision/order. The Commissioner (Appeals) may allow a further period of 30 days if satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause.
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 128(1)

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962 , what percentage of the duty demanded or penalty imposed must be pre-deposited before filing an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals)?
explain: Under Section 129E(i), an appeal before Commissioner (Appeals) under Section ₹28 cannot be entertained unless the appellant has pre-deposited 7.5% of the duty demanded or penalty imposed (subject to a maximum ceiling of Rs. ₹0 Crores).
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129E(i)

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: What is the mandatory pre-deposit percentage required under Section 129E(iii) when appealing to the CESTAT against an order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals)?
explain: Under Section 129E(iii), for filing an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) against an order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals), the appellant must deposit ₹0 % of the duty demanded or penalty imposed, capped at Rs. ₹0 Crores.
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129E(iii)

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under the first proviso to Section 129A(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , which of the following matters is expressly barred from being heard by the CESTAT?
options: Confiscation of gold and precious metals exceeding ₹50 Lakhs
Orders passed by Commissioner (Appeals) relating to baggage, short-landing in transit, and drawback
Valuation disputes under the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007
explain: The first proviso to Section 129A(1) bars CESTAT from hearing appeals against orders of Commissioner (Appeals) relating to: (a) any goods imported/exported as baggage, (b) goods loaded in a conveyance for import but short-landed, and (c) payment of drawback. These disputes lie exclusively by Revision Application to the Central Government under Section 129DD.
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129A(1) First Proviso

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 129DD of the Customs Act, 1962 , a Revision Application to the Central Government against an order of the Commissioner (Appeals) must be filed within what period?
options: 6 months from the date of the order
3 months from date of communication (extendable by further 3 months)
explain: Under Section 129DD(2), an application for revision must be made within 3 months from the date of communication of the order. The Central Government may extend this period by a further 3 months if satisfied there was sufficient cause.
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 129DD

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹04 of the Customs Act, 1962 , an offence is categorized as cognizable and non-bailable only if the duty evasion, fraudulent drawback, or value of prohibited goods exceeds:
explain: Under Section ₹04 (4) & (6) as amended, customs offences are non-cognizable and bailable, EXCEPT where the market price of prohibited goods or evasion of duty/fraudulent drawback exceeds ₹50 Lakhs (or specified unauthorized importation/exportation exceeds ₹1 Crore), in which case they become cognizable and non-bailable.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 104(4) & (6)

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹35 (1)(i) of the Customs Act, 1962 , for an offence involving duty evasion exceeding ₹50 Lakhs, the offender is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to:
options: 7 years and with fine (with a minimum sentence of 1 year in the absence of special reasons)
explain: Section ₹35 (1)(i) prescribes imprisonment up to 7 years and fine for duty evasion or fraudulent drawback exceeding ₹50 Lakhs (or relating to prohibited goods). In the absence of special and adequate reasons recorded in the judgment, the imprisonment shall not be for less than 1 year.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 135(1)(i)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Where the proper officer re-assesses duty under Section ₹7 (4) contrary to self-assessment, within how many days must a speaking order be passed if the importer has not confirmed acceptance in writing?
options: 30 days from the date of re-assessment
₹5 days from the date of re-assessment
explain: Under Section ₹7 (5) of the Customs Act, 1962 , where any re-assessment done under sub-section (4) is contrary to the self-assessment and the importer/exporter does not confirm acceptance in writing, the proper officer shall pass a speaking order within ₹5 days from the date of re-assessment of the bill of entry or the shipping bill.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 17(5)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: When a provisional duty assessment is finalized under Section ₹8 (2) and the importer is liable to pay differential duty, from which date is interest payable under Section ₹8 (3)?
options: From the first day of the month in which duty was provisionally assessed till the date of payment
From the date of filing the original Bill of Entry
From the date of the final assessment order
From 3 months after the provisional assessment date
explain: Section ₹8 (3) mandates that the importer shall be liable to pay interest on any differential duty from the first day of the month in which duty was provisionally assessed till the date of payment thereof, at the rate fixed under Section 28AA (currently ₹5 % p.a.).
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 18(3)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
section: Section 18(1A) & Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regs, 2018
text: Under the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2018, what is the primary time limit within which a provisional assessment must be finalized by the proper officer?
options: 2 years from the date of provisional assessment (extendable by Commissioner by 1 year)
6 months from the date of provisional assessment
1 year from the date of provisional assessment
explain: Under Section ₹8 (1A) and the 2018 Regulations, provisional assessment must be finalized within 2 years from the date of provisional assessment. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may extend this period by a further period not exceeding 1 year on sufficient cause shown.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 18(1A) & Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regs, 2018

chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
text: Under the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, for what minimum duration is an auditee required to preserve and maintain all customs-related books of accounts, records, and electronic data?
options: 5 years from the date of clearance of goods
3 years from end of the financial year
explain: Regulation 3 of the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018 mandates that an auditee shall preserve and maintain all records, books of account, and data related to customs transactions for a minimum period of 5 years from the date of clearance of goods.
topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Section 99A & Customs Audit Regulations, 2018

chapter: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment
text: Before conducting a Premises-Based Audit (PBA) at the business premises of an auditee under Section 99A, what is the minimum advance notice required to be served by the proper officer?
options: No notice is required; surprise visits are statutory
explain: Under Regulation 4(1) of the Customs Audit Regulations, 2018, the proper officer shall give not less than ₹5 days advance notice in writing to the auditee before conducting an audit at their premises.
topic: Chapter 10: Examination of Goods, Risk Management and Faceless Assessment — Regulation 4, Customs Audit Regulations, 2018

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
section: Section 46(3) & Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration) Regs, 2018
text: Under Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 read with CBIC regulations, what are the prescribed late charges for delay in presenting a Bill of Entry?
options: ₹2,500 per day up to 7 days, and ₹5,000 thereafter
₹5,000 per day for the initial 3 days, and Rs. ₹0,000 per day for each subsequent day
₹1,000 per day for all days of delay
Flat Rs. ₹0,000 irrespective of the number of days
explain: Under Section 46(3) and Notification No. 36/2018-Customs (N.T.), late filing fees are levied at ₹5,000 per day for the first 3 days of delay following the arrival deadline, and Rs. ₹0,000 per day for each subsequent day of delay.
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3) & Bill of Entry (Electronic Integrated Declaration) Regs, 2018

chapter: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations
text: Under the second proviso to Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 , an advance or prior Bill of Entry may be presented up to how many days before the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft?
explain: Under the second proviso to Section 46(3) of the Customs Act, 1962 (as amended by Finance Act 2018 and Notification 36/2018-Cus), a Bill of Entry may be presented at any time not exceeding 30 days prior to the expected arrival of the vessel or aircraft.
topic: Chapter 3: Preparation of Bills of Entry, Shipping Bills and Baggage Declarations — Section 46(3) Second Proviso

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962 , if imported goods are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused within what statutory timeframe from unloading, may the custodian proceed to sell them after giving notice?
explain: Section 48 provides that if any goods brought into India from outside are not cleared for home consumption or warehoused within 30 days from the date of unloading (or such extended time as allowed by the proper officer), the custodian may, with customs permission, sell them after giving notice to the importer.
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 48

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 6(4) of CBLR 2018, a candidate is permitted a maximum of how many attempts within what period from the date of application?
options: Unlimited attempts until the age of 50 years
explain: Under Regulation 6(4) of CBLR 2018, the applicant shall be allowed a maximum of 6 attempts within a period of 7 years from the date of application both the written and oral examinations.
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 6(4)

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 7(2) of CBLR 2018, a Customs Broker license granted in Form B is valid for a period of:
options: Lifetime validity with annual renewal fees
₹0 years (renewable for ₹0 years at a time)
explain: Under Regulation 7(2) of the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018, a license granted under Regulation 7 shall be valid for a period of ₹0 years from the date of issue, and may be renewed for further periods of ₹0 years at a time.
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 7(2)

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation ₹0 (n) of CBLR 2018, what is the mandatory obligation of a Customs Broker regarding client verification?
options: Conduct a physical site inspection with two local witnesses and a notary
Verify the correctness of IEC, identity of client, and functioning of client at declared address using reliable, independent source documents
Request a police verification certificate prior to taking up customs work
Obtain a simple signed letter on the client's letterhead
explain: Regulation ₹0 (n) mandates that a Customs Broker shall verify the correctness of the Importer Exporter Code (IEC) number, identity of client and functioning of client at the declared address by using reliable, independent, authentic documents, data or information (KYC norms).
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 10(n)

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 13 of CBLR 2018, what is the functional difference between a 'G-card' holder and an 'H-card' holder?
options: G-card holders are permanent partners; H-card holders are temporary apprentices
G-card holders handle ocean customs; H-card holders handle air customs
G-card holders have passed the Reg ₹3 exam and can sign declarations; H-card holders are non-exam clerks who assist and cannot sign declarations
There is no functional difference; they denote different customs ports
explain: Under Regulation 13 , employees who qualify the examination under Regulation 13 are issued a 'G-card' authorising them to sign customs declarations. Other non-qualified assistants are issued an 'H-card' valid for assisting in movement and examination of cargo without authority to sign legal customs declarations.
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 13(1), (5) & (6)

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: Under Regulation 18 of the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018, what is the maximum penalty that a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may impose on a Customs Broker for contravention of any provision?
explain: Regulation 18 of CBLR 2018 provides that the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may impose a penalty not exceeding ₹50,000 on a Customs Broker who contravenes any of the provisions of these regulations.
topic: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 — Regulation 18

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under General Rule of Interpretation 2(a), how is an incomplete or unfinished article classified if presented unassembled or disassembled (CKD/SKD)?
options: Classified under the heading appearing last in numerical order
Classified as parts and accessories under their respective headings
Classified as the complete or finished article, provided it has the essential character of the complete article
Classified under the residual heading of as project cargo
explain: GIR 2(a) states: 'Any reference in a heading to an article shall be taken to include a reference to that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that, as presented, the incomplete or unfinished article has the essential character of the complete or finished article. It shall also be taken to include a reference to that article complete or finished ... presented unassembled or disassembled.'
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 2(a)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under GIR 3(a), when goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, the rule of preference dictates that:
options: The importer may freely select whichever heading carries the lowest rate of duty
The heading providing the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description
The heading carrying the lower numerical code takes automatic precedence
The heading carrying the highest duty rate shall always be applied
explain: GIR 3(a) provides: 'The heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description.' However, when two or more headings each refer to part only of materials, those headings are regarded as equally specific.
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 3(a)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under GIR 3(b), composite goods consisting of different materials or goods put up in sets for retail sale are classified based on:
options: The component that is mentioned first in the commercial packing list
The heading that carries the lowest basic customs duty
The component which gives them their essential character
The component that represents more than 50% of the total invoice value
explain: GIR 3(b) explicitly provides that mixtures, composite goods consisting of different materials or made up of different components, and goods put up in sets for retail sale, which cannot be classified by reference to 3(a), shall be classified as if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their essential character.
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 3(b)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: When goods cannot be classified by reference to Rule 3(a) or 3(b), how are they classified under Rule 3(c)?
options: Under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration
By statutory determination of the Settlement Commission
Under the heading occurring first in numerical order among those meriting consideration
explain: GIR 3(c) states: 'When goods cannot be classified by reference to (a) or (b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration.'
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 3(c)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under GIR 5(a), camera cases, musical instrument cases, and specially shaped containers entered with the articles they are intended to contain are classified:
options: Free of duty as non-dutiable packaging assists
Always separately under as articles of leather/plastics
With such articles, if they are of a kind normally sold therewith and suitable for long-term use, unless the container gives the whole its essential character
explain: GIR 5(a) provides that cases shaped or fitted to contain a specific article or set of articles, suitable for long-term use and presented with the articles for which they are intended, shall be classified with such articles when of a kind normally sold therewith. This rule does not apply to containers giving the whole its essential character.
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — GIR 5(a)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: What is the normal limitation period for the proper officer to issue a Show Cause Notice for non-levy, short-levy, or erroneous refund of customs duty under Section 28(1) in the absence of fraud or collusion?
options: 3 years from the end of the financial year
explain: Under Section 28(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 (as amended by Finance Act 2016), the normal limitation period for issuing a notice for duty not levied, short-levied, or erroneously refunded is 2 years from the relevant date.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(1)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 28(4) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the limitation period for demanding duty where non-levy or short-levy is by reason of collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts?
options: ₹0 years from the date of clearance
explain: Section 28(4) provides that where duty has not been levied, has been short-levied or erroneously refunded by reason of collusion, any wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts by the importer or exporter, the limitation period to issue a notice is 5 years from the relevant date.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(4)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 28(5) of the Customs Act, 1962 , if an assessee pays the duty demanded under Section 28(4) along with interest within 30 days of receipt of the notice, what is the reduced penalty payable?
explain: Under Section 28(5) of the Customs Act, 1962 , where the duty specified in the notice under sub-section (4) is paid along with interest within 30 days of the receipt of the notice, the penalty payable shall be ₹5 % of the duty, and all proceedings in respect of the said duty and interest shall be deemed to be concluded.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 28(5)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 74(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what percentage of import duty paid is admissible as drawback when duty-paid imported goods are entered for export without having been used in India?
explain: Under Section 74(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , when goods capable of being easily identified which have been imported into India and upon which duties have been paid are exported without having been used, 98% of such duty shall be repaid as drawback.
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(1)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Notification No. ₹9 /65-Customs as amended, what is the maximum period of use of goods in India beyond which drawback under Section 74 is completely nil?
explain: Under Section 74(2) read with Notification No. ₹9 /65-Customs as amended, drawback on imported goods used before re-export is progressively reduced, and is explicitly NIL if the period between the date of clearance for home consumption and the date of export exceeds 36 months (3 years).
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 74(2) & Notification 19/65-Customs

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 76(1)(c) of the Customs Act, 1962 , no drawback shall be allowed in respect of any goods if the amount of drawback claimed is less than:
explain: Section 76(1)(c) of the Customs Act, 1962 provides that no drawback shall be allowed in respect of any goods where the amount of drawback in respect of any single claim is less than ₹50.
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 76(1)(c)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, an application for determination of Brand Rate of duty drawback must be filed within what timeframe from the date of export (LEO)?
options: 1 year from the date of shipping bill
3 months (extendable by a further 3 months on payment of fee)
explain: Under Rule 6(1) and Rule 7(1) of the Drawback Rules 2017, the manufacturer-exporter must apply for Brand Rate fixation within 3 months from the relevant export date. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs may extend this period by a further 3 months on sufficient cause and payment of prescribed late fee.
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Rule 6 & Rule 7

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹10 of the Finance Act, 2018, what is the rate of Social Welfare Surcharge (SWS) levied on imported goods, and on what value is it calculated?
options: 4% calculated on basic customs duty plus IGST
₹0 % calculated on the aggregate of all duties of customs levied under Section ₹2 (excluding IGST and Compensation Cess)
₹0 % calculated on the assessable CIF value of the goods
explain: Section ₹10 of the Finance Act, 2018 levies Social Welfare Surcharge at ₹0 % on the aggregate duties of customs levied under Section ₹2 of the Customs Act, 1962 . It is not calculated on assessable value, and IGST under Sec 3(7) and Compensation Cess under Sec 3(9) of CTA 1975 are statutorily excluded from the SWS base.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110, Finance Act, 2018

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Section 9A(5) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , for how long does an Anti-Dumping Duty remain in force from the date of its imposition, unless revoked earlier?
explain: Under Section 9A(5) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , Anti-Dumping Duty ceases to have effect on the expiry of 5 years from the date of its imposition. If the Central Government initiates a sunset review before the expiry, the duty may remain in force pending review for a period up to 1 year.
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9A(5)

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty
text: Under Section 9A(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 , what is the maximum duration for which a provisional Anti-Dumping Duty may be imposed pending final determination?
options: 6 months (extendable to 9 months by Central Government upon request)
explain: Section 9A(2) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 provides that provisional anti-dumping duty shall remain in force for a period not exceeding 6 months, which may, upon request of exporters representing a significant percentage of trade, be extended by the Central Government to 9 months.
topic: Chapter 5: Tariff Classification and Rates of Duty — Section 9A(2)

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Para 5.01 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023, what is the Export Obligation (EO) requirement under the zero-duty EPCG scheme for imported capital goods?
options: ₹0 times the duty saved in 8 years
Equal to the CIF value of imported capital goods within 3 years
6 times the duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled in 6 years from authorization date
8 times the FOB value within 5 years
explain: Under Para 5.01 of FTP 2023, import of capital goods for pre-production, production, and post-production is allowed at zero customs duty under the EPCG Scheme subject to an Export Obligation equivalent to 6 times the duty saved on capital goods, to be fulfilled within 6 years from authorization date.
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Para 5.01, Foreign Trade Policy 2023

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Para 4.08 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023, what is the minimum mandatory Value Addition required for exports under an Advance Authorization (except for tea)?
explain: Para 4.08 of FTP 2023 stipulates that a minimum ₹5 % value addition shall be required for issuance of an Advance Authorization, except for export of tea where the minimum value addition requirement is 50%.
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Para 4.08, Foreign Trade Policy 2023

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments
text: Under Para 1.25 of FTP 2023, what is the export performance threshold (in USD equivalent) required to obtain 'One Star Export House' status?
explain: Under FTP 2023 Para 1.25, the thresholds in US Dollars FOB/FOR during current and previous three financial years are: One Star = $3 Million, Two Star = $₹5 Million, Three Star = $50 Million, Four Star = $200 Million, Five Star = $800 Million.
topic: Chapter 21: High-Frequency Miscellany - Monitoring Systems, Trade Instruments — Para 1.25, Foreign Trade Policy 2023

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under Notification No. ₹9 /2023-Customs (N.T.), which of the following categories of import goods is EXEMPTED from the mandatory payment of customs duties through the Electronic Cash Ledger (ECL)?
options: Commercial containers cleared through inland container depots (ICDs)
Goods imported through courier or postal channels, and passenger baggage
Goods imported under the EPCG scheme
explain: Notification No. ₹9 /2023-Customs (N.T.) specifically exempts passenger baggage, goods imported/exported through international courier or postal routes, and non-EDI manual bills from the mandatory ECL mechanism under Section 51A.
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — Section 51A & Notification No. 19/2023-Customs (N.T.)

act: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Customs (ICEGATE / EDI)
chapter: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing
text: Under the e-SANCHIT paperless customs initiative, what document identifier is generated when a supporting document is successfully uploaded by an authorized signatory using digital signature?
options: Goods and Services Tax Identification Number (GSTIN)
explain: Under e-SANCHIT (Circular 40/2017-Cus), when an importer or Customs Broker uploads a digitally signed PDF supporting document on ICEGATE, the system validates the digital signature and generates a unique Image Reference Number (IRN), which is then quoted in the Bill of Entry.
topic: Chapter 19: Electronic Data Interchange, ICEGATE and Online Filing — CBIC Circular No. 40/2017-Customs

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: In a High Sea Sale transaction where goods are sold prior to customs clearance, on what value is customs duty assessed on the ultimate high sea buyer?
options: The minimum tariff value notified by DGFT
The average of the original invoice price and high sea sales invoice price
The final high sea sale value paid by the ultimate buyer (including high sea sales margin/commission)
The original foreign supplier invoice value paid by the first importer
explain: In high sea sales, the actual transaction value under Section ₹4 is the price paid by the final buyer who files the Bill of Entry for home consumption, which encompasses the original CIF cost plus the high sea seller's mark-up/commission (Circular No. 32/2004-Cus).
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Section 14 & CBIC Circular No. 32/2004-Cus

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Rule 6 of the IGCR Rules, 2022, by which date of each succeeding month must an importer submit the monthly statement in Form IGCR-3 on the common portal?
options: By the 10th day of the succeeding month
By the last day of the succeeding quarter
By the 20th day of the succeeding month
By the 5th day of the succeeding month
explain: Rule 6(1) of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022 requires the importer to submit a monthly statement in Form IGCR-3 electronically on the common portal by the 10th day of the following month.
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Rule 6, IGCR Rules 2022

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under Rule 7(1) of the IPR (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules, 2007, once the proper officer suspends clearance of suspected counterfeit goods, within how many days must the right holder join proceedings?
options: ₹0 working days for normal goods, and 3 working days for perishable goods
3 working days for normal goods, 24 hours for perishables
explain: Under Rule 7(1) of IPR Rules 2007, the right holder shall join the proceedings within a period of ₹0 working days (or 3 working days in the case of perishable goods) from the date of notice of suspension of clearance, failing which the goods are released to the importer.
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 7(1)

chapter: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies
text: Under Rule 9 of the IPR Enforcement Rules, 2007, can counterfeit trademark goods or pirated copyright goods be released to the importer on payment of a redemption fine?
options: Yes, if the counterfeit marks are erased with customs permission
Yes, upon payment of double the standard redemption fine under Section ₹25
Yes, provided the brand owner receives 50% of the auction proceeds
No; counterfeit goods cannot be released into commercial channels even with consent, and must be destroyed or disposed of outside commerce
explain: Rule 9 explicitly prohibits the release of infringing goods to the importer upon payment of fine or duty, and prohibits re-exportation in unaltered state. Counterfeit goods must be destroyed or disposed of outside channels of commerce under customs supervision.
topic: Chapter 16: Allied Acts and Participating Government Agencies — Rule 9

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, pre-packaged commodities imported into India are EXEMPT from retail MRP labeling declarations if:
options: The goods are packaged in containers of less than ₹00 grams
The goods are cleared through an Inland Container Depot (ICD)
The goods originate from SAARC preferential trade countries
The packages are meant strictly for industrial consumers or institutional consumers
explain: Under Rule 3 of the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, packages intended for industrial consumers (who buy directly for manufacturing) or institutional consumers (hospitals, railways, hotels) are exempt from Chapter II retail declarations including MRP.
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 3, Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under the first proviso to Section 114A of the Customs Act, 1962 , where an equal penalty is imposed for collusion, willful misstatement or suppression under Section 114A:
options: The Commissioner must obtain CESTAT approval before recovery
The prosecution under Section ₹35 is automatically barred
No penalty shall be imposed on the person under Section ₹12 or Section ₹14
A parallel penalty under Section ₹12 or Section ₹14 shall also be levied mandatorily
explain: The first proviso to Section 114A explicitly bars double jeopardy by providing that where penalty is imposed under Section 114A, no penalty under Section ₹12 (improper importation) or Section ₹14 (improper exportation) shall be imposed on the same person for the same offence.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114A First Proviso

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section 114AA of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the maximum penalty for intentionally using a false or incorrect declaration, statement, or forged document in customs business?
options: Up to equal to the duty evaded
Up to five times the value of the goods
explain: Section 114AA provides that if any person intentionally makes, signs or uses any declaration, statement or document which is false or incorrect in any material particular, he shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five times the value of the goods.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 114AA

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹25 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the statutory ceiling on the fine that may be imposed in lieu of confiscation (redemption fine)?
options: The market price of the goods confiscated, less the duty chargeable thereon
Double the amount of basic customs duty
The assessable CIF value of the goods
explain: The proviso to Section ₹25 (1) mandates that the fine in lieu of confiscation shall not exceed the market price of the goods confiscated, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable thereon.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 125(1) Proviso

chapter: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers
text: Under Section ₹3 of the Customs Act, 1962 , an importer is NOT liable to pay customs duty on pilfered goods, provided the pilferage occurred:
options: Before the bill of lading was endorsed by the shipping line
At any time while the goods are lying in a public bonded warehouse
While the vessel was carrying goods on the high seas
After the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or warehousing
explain: Section ₹3 provides that if any imported goods are pilfered after the unloading thereof and before the proper officer has made an order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, the importer shall not be liable to pay duty. Once out-of-charge or in-bond order is made, Section ₹3 does not apply.
topic: Chapter 2: The Customs Act, 1962 - Framework, Definitions and Officers — Section 13

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 23(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner shall remit duty on imported goods if it is proved that the goods have been lost or destroyed:
options: Only after filing a formal insurance subrogation claim
Only if the loss is due to enemy action or war
Only before the goods are unloaded from the ship
At any time before clearance for home consumption, including while in a customs warehouse
explain: Section 23(1) applies to goods lost (other than as a result of pilferage) or destroyed by accident at ANY time before clearance for home consumption, including while warehoused under Chapter IX. Duty on such goods shall be remitted by the proper officer.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(1)

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under the proviso to Section 23(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 , an owner of imported goods is PROHIBITED from relinquishing title to the goods if:
options: The goods are packaged in wooden crates
Any offence appears to have been committed under this Act or any other law in respect of such goods
The assessable value of the consignment exceeds Rs. ₹0 Lakhs
The goods have been lying uncleared for more than ₹5 days
explain: The proviso to Section 23(2) clearly states: 'Provided that the owner of any such imported goods shall not be allowed to relinquish his title to such goods regarding which an offence appears to have been committed under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.'
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 23(2) Proviso

chapter: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds
text: Under Section 27(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , what is the limitation period for an importer to claim a refund of customs duty, and where is the refund credited if unjust enrichment is not rebutted?
options: 2 years; refunded to the shipping agent
3 years; credited to the Port Trust Authority
1 year from date of payment; credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund under Section 12C of Central Excise Act
6 months; credited to the Consolidated Fund of India
explain: Section 27(1) prescribes 1 year limitation from payment date. Under Section 27(2), the refund is statutorily credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund established under Section 12C of the Central Excise Act, ₹944 , unless the applicant proves that the incidence of duty had not been passed on to any other person.
topic: Chapter 9: Assessment, Payment of Duty, Demands and Refunds — Section 27(1) & (2)

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹02 (1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , when an officer is about to search any person under Section ₹00 or ₹01 , what statutory right must the officer inform the person of?
options: The right to be taken without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate
The right to refuse search until a judicial warrant is produced
The right to conduct self-search in the presence of a doctor
The right to call a legal practitioner immediately
explain: Section ₹02 (1) mandates that when an officer of customs is about to search any person under Section ₹00 or ₹01 , he shall, if such person so requires, take him without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer of Customs or Magistrate.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 102(1)

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section ₹08 (4) of the Customs Act, 1962 , every inquiry conducted by an officer summoning a person is deemed to be a:
options: Judicial proceeding within the meaning of Sections ₹93 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
Summary trial before a Sessions Court
Commercial dispute subject to the Arbitration and Conciliation Act
Confidential departmental inquiry without legal consequence
explain: Section ₹08 (4) provides that every inquiry under Section ₹08 shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section ₹93 and section 228 of the Indian Penal Code. Giving false evidence or refusing to answer is punishable as perjury.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 108(4)

chapter: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest
text: Under Section 110A of the Customs Act, 1962 , who is the authority empowered to order provisional release of any goods seized under Section ₹10 pending adjudication?
options: The High Court having territorial jurisdiction
The Adjudicating Authority, on taking a bond from the owner with such security and conditions as may be required
explain: Section 110A provides that any goods, documents or things seized under Section ₹10 may, pending the order of the adjudicating authority, be released to the owner upon taking a bond from him in the proper form with such security and conditions as the adjudicating authority may require.
topic: Chapter 15: Offences, Penal Provisions, Search, Seizure and Arrest — Section 110A

chapter: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution
text: Under Section 127B(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 , an application for settlement of a case can be made only if the additional amount of duty accepted by the applicant exceeds:
explain: Under Section 127B(1) first proviso, no application shall be made unless the applicant has filed a bill of entry or shipping bill, received a show cause notice, and the additional amount of duty accepted by the applicant in his application exceeds three lakh rupees.
topic: Chapter 18: Appeals, Revision and Dispute Resolution — Section 127B(1) First Proviso

act: Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 & FTP 2023
chapter: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones
text: Under Section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, when any goods are removed from a Special Economic Zone to the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), what duties are chargeable?
options: A flat compounding tax of 5% on factory gate value
Nil duty, as both are situated within the geographical boundaries of India
Only Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST)
Customs duties including Basic Customs Duty, IGST, anti-dumping duty and countervailing duty, as if imported into India
explain: Under Section 30 of the SEZ Act, 2005, any goods removed from an SEZ to the DTA shall be chargeable to duties of customs, including basic customs duty, integrated tax, compensation cess and anti-dumping duty, at the rate in force on the date of removal.
topic: Chapter 14: Drawback, Export Promotion Schemes and Special Economic Zones — Section 30, SEZ Act, 2005 & Rule 47

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under the first proviso to Rule ₹0 (2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, where goods are imported by air, what is the statutory ceiling on the cost of transportation/freight to be added to FOB value?
options: Actual air freight regardless of amount
Cannot exceed ₹0 % of the CIF value
Cannot exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods
explain: Under the first proviso to Rule ₹0 (2) of CVR 2007, where goods are imported by air, the cost of transport added to FOB value shall not exceed 20% of the FOB value of the goods, even if the actual air freight paid is higher.
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) First Proviso

act: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 & Valuation Rules
chapter: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods
text: Under Rule ₹0 (2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2007, where the cost of insurance is not ascertainable, what percentage of FOB value must be added to determine assessable value?
explain: Under the third proviso to Rule ₹0 (2) of CVR 2007, where the cost of insurance is not ascertainable, it shall be calculated at 1.₹25 % of the FOB value of the goods.
topic: Chapter 6: Valuation of Imported and Export Goods — Rule 10(2) Third Proviso

chapter: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR
text: Under Section 58A of the Customs Act, 1962 , 'Special Warehouses' subject to physical locking and control by the proper officer are specifically for:
options: Duty-free shop supplies, ship stores, aviation fuel, and other notified sensitive goods
Automobile raw materials under the EPCG scheme
explain: Section 58A provides for licensing of special warehouses wherein the lock of the proper officer is maintained on the warehouse. Under Notification No. 66/2016-Cus (N.T.), goods notified include duty-free shop goods, supply as stores to vessels/aircraft, and crude petroleum.
topic: Chapter 12: Warehousing, Bonding and Clearance from Bond; MOOWR — Section 58A

Two years experience in transacting Customs Broker work as a G-Card holder

Shall not be required to appear for any further examination
Must appear only for the written examination

₹25,000 within sixty days of clearing the written exam
₹10,000 within one month of result declaration

text: Under Regulation 7(3) of CBLR 2018, a licensed Customs Broker wishing to transact business at another customs station must submit an intimation in:
explain: Regulation 7(3) mandates that a Customs Broker holding a valid licence may transact business in other customs stations by submitting an intimation in Form C to the Commissioner of Customs of that station.

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018

chapter: Chapter 1: Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018
text: The security to be furnished under Regulation 8 is for an amount of:

The Customs Broker has paid all dues and no proceedings are pending
The licence has been suspended earlier
